metadata.authors: Christian Kanzow, Daniel Steck, Daniel Wachsmuth
metadata.title:
An Augmented Lagrangian Method for Optimization Problems in Banach
  Spaces
metadata.abstract:
We propose a variant of the classical augmented Lagrangian method for
constrained optimization problems in Banach spaces. Our theoretical framework
does not require any convexity or second-order assumptions and allows the
treatment of inequality constraints with infinite-dimensional image space.
Moreover, we discuss the convergence properties of our algorithm with regard to
feasibility, global optimality, and KKT conditions. Some numerical results are
given to illustrate the practical viability of the method.

abstract.text:
We propose a variant of the classical augmented Lagrangian method for
constrained optimization problems in Banach spaces. Our theoretical framework
does not require any convexity or second-order assumptions and allows the
treatment of inequality constraints with infinite-dimensional image space.
Moreover, we discuss the convergence properties of our algorithm with regard to
feasibility, global optimality, and KKT conditions. Some numerical results are
given to illustrate the practical viability of the method.

Introduction.text:
Let X, Y be (real) Banach spaces and let f:X\rightarrow \mathbb {R}, g:X\rightarrow Y be
given mappings. The aim of this paper is to describe an augmented Lagrangian
method for the solution of the constrained optimization problem\min \ f(x) \quad \text{subject to (s.t.)}\quad g(x)\le 0.We assume that Y\hookrightarrow L^2(\Omega ) densely for some measure space
\Omega , where the natural order on L^2(\Omega ) induces the order on Y. A
detailed description together with some remarks about this setting is given in
Section 2.Augmented Lagrangian methods for the solution of optimization problems
belong to the most famous and successful algorithms for the
solution of finite-dimensional problems and are
described in almost all text books on continuous optimization, see, e.g. {{cite:40fec8245775d40371b9097ecfd54b9b09d9181a}}, {{cite:ea8f543bb72e77cbc893fe2a79f5430dc637360c}}. Their
generalization to infinite-dimensional problems has received considerable
attention throughout the last decades {{cite:c84e3bc1f1cff9489c2a8ca2ed3f4672b053ebb2}}, {{cite:4948894d969704c26162ebd4d51001867126c6f3}}, {{cite:98e16c9b56b6025138e508bc39b425f18d947678}}, {{cite:fb89da83a293fbcadc88c0b74e4f3f36b60f130d}}, {{cite:8d9d203b1b1078fb5f97bac934acded367791bb7}}, {{cite:50085ef420cdb0b9926b1f1ab48b609ae7a5eb72}}, {{cite:666357c04a04ad47fbf3d39ba06d8ec0a5bbe25c}}, {{cite:bfdd7496db4d92a5389084308f3980882faad511}}, {{cite:d8d120c076063b7a75411226fa2310ba0b639686}}. However,
most existing approaches either assume a very specific problem structure
{{cite:c84e3bc1f1cff9489c2a8ca2ed3f4672b053ebb2}}, {{cite:4948894d969704c26162ebd4d51001867126c6f3}}, require strong convexity assumptions
{{cite:fb89da83a293fbcadc88c0b74e4f3f36b60f130d}} or consider only the case where Y is finite-dimensional
{{cite:8d9d203b1b1078fb5f97bac934acded367791bb7}}, {{cite:bfdd7496db4d92a5389084308f3980882faad511}}.The contribution of the present paper is to overcome these limitations and
to provide a general convergence theory for infinite-dimensional problems.
To this end, we extend some of the recent contributions on the convergence of
certain modified augmented Lagrangian methods from the finite- to the
infinite-dimensional case, cf. {{cite:2bb4d3bb8ed1e7fcf9f019be0b6c81ed83196451}} and references therein
for more details regarding some of the newer convergence results in the
finite-dimensional setting. The main difference between the classical
augmented Lagrangian approach and its modified version consists
of a more controlled way of the multiplier update which is responsible
for a stronger global convergence theory.Clearly, the main application of our theoretical framework (REF ) is
constrained optimization in function spaces, where the inequality constraint
with Y\hookrightarrow L^2(\Omega ) arises naturally. In particular, our
theory covers obstacle-type problems as well as optimal control problems
(including semilinear partial differential equations) with state constraints.Let us remark that our algorithm can also be viewed as an extension of the quadratic penalty method (also called Moreau-Yosida regularization in the infinite-dimensional literature, e.g. {{cite:fb89da83a293fbcadc88c0b74e4f3f36b60f130d}}, {{cite:bbddb591dafd85fd8abccba19780d1b2ff384976}}). A numerical comparison to this method is given in Section .This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we give a detailed overview
of our problem setting and assumptions. Section 3 contains a precise statement
of the algorithm, and we conduct a convergence analysis dedicated to global
optimization in Section 4. Starting with Section 5, we assume that the mappings
which constitute our problem are continuously differentiable, and establish some
theoretical foundations regarding KKT conditions and constraint qualifications.
In Section 6, we apply these insights to our algorithm and deduce corresponding
convergence results. Finally, Section 7 contains practical applications and we
conclude with some final remarks in Section 8.Notation: We use standard notation such as \left\langle \cdot ,\cdot  \right\rangle  for the
duality pairing on Y, \left( \cdot ,\cdot  \right)_Z for the scalar product in the Hilbert space
Z, and \perp  to denote orthogonality in Z. Moreover, \mathcal {L}(X,Y) denotes the
space of continuous linear operators from X into Y. The norms on X, Y, etc. are
denoted by \Vert \cdot \Vert , where an index (as in \Vert \cdot \Vert _X) is appended if necessary.
Furthermore, we write \rightarrow , \rightharpoonup , and \rightharpoonup ^* for strong, weak, and weak-^*
convergence, respectively. Finally, we use the abbreviation lsc for a lower
semicontinuous function.

Preliminaries and Assumptions.text:
We denote by e:Y\rightarrow Z the (linear and continuous) dense embedding of Y into
Z:=L^2(\Omega ), and by K_Y, K_Z the respective nonnegative cones in
Y and Z, i.e.K_Z:=\lbrace z\in Z\mid z(t)\ge 0~\text{a.e.}\rbrace  \quad \text{and}\quad K_Y:= \lbrace  y\in Y \mid e(y) \in K_Z\rbrace .Note that the adjoint mapping e^* embeds Z^* into Y^*. Hence, we have
the chainY \hookrightarrow Z \cong Z^* \hookrightarrow Y^*,which is occasionally referred to as a Gelfand triple.
The main reason for the specific configuration of our spaces Y and Z is
that the order on Z=L^2(\Omega ) has some structural properties which
may not hold on Y. For instance, the L^2-norm satisfies the relation0 \le z_1 \le z_2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \Vert z_1\Vert _Z \le \Vert z_2\Vert _Z,which does not hold for, say, the spaces H^1 or H_0^1. (Note that
(REF ) is one of the defining properties of so-called
Banach or Hilbert lattices {{cite:b8dc03b226a5c6f4e5aceb7813665d63b15d15d6}}, {{cite:1dbcd2a416bde9a207323b83adb21c7f7ab0eaed}}. In fact,
Z=L^2(\Omega ) is a Hilbert lattice, but H^1(\Omega ) and H_0^1(\Omega )
are not.) We will put the properties of Z to fruitful use by performing
the augmentation which constitutes our algorithm in Z. To simplify this,
we denote by z_+ and z_- the positive and negative parts of z\in Z,
i.e.z_+ := \max \lbrace z,0\rbrace  \quad \text{and}\quad z_- := \max \lbrace -z,0\rbrace .These operations have a variety of useful properties. For instance, we have
z=z_+-z_- and z_+ \perp z_- for every z\in Z.Recall that, as in the introduction, we are concerned with the optimization
problem\min \ f(x) \quad \text{s.t.}\quad g(x)\le 0,where Y\hookrightarrow Z=L^2(\Omega ). Here, the inequality g(x)\le 0 has to
be understood with respect to the order induced by the cone K_Y, which is
implicitly given by the order on Z through the embedding e.The following is a list of assumptions which we will use throughout this paper.Assumption 2.1 (General assumptions on the problem
setting)f and \Vert g_+\Vert _Z are weakly lower semicontinuous.

f and g are continuously Fréchet-differentiable.

y\mapsto |y| is well-defined and continuous on Y.

The unit ball in Y^* is weak-^* sequentially
compact.Most of the theorems we will encounter later use only a subset of these
assumptions. Hence, we will usually list the assumptions for each theorem
explicitly by referencing to the names REF -REF .One assumption which might require some elaboration is the weak lower
semicontinuity of \Vert g_+\Vert _Z. To this end, note that there are various
theorems which characterize the weak lower semicontinuity of convex functions,
e.g. {{cite:ec4ff414cc400c0bc601f8a04783b4b9e8f7ad22}}. Hence, if \Vert g_+\Vert  is convex (which is true if g is convex with respect to the order in Y), then
the (strong) lower semicontinuity of g already implies the weak lower
semicontinuity. We conclude that (A1) holds, in particular, for every
lsc. convex function  f  and any mapping g\in \mathcal {L}(X,Y).On a further note, the above remarks offer another criterion for the weak
lower semicontinuity of \Vert g_+\Vert _Z. Since y\mapsto \Vert y_+\Vert  obviously has
this property, we conclude that it is sufficient for g to be weakly
(sequentially) continuous.Regarding the space Y which is embedded into Z, recall that
REF  assumed the operation y\mapsto |y| to be well-defined and
continuous on Y. (Note that this assumption holds automatically if
 Y = Z , but in many applications,  Y  is only a subset of  Z , cf. the first remark below.) Hence,
the same holds for the mappings y_+, y_-, \min , \max , etc., which may
be defined in terms of their counterparts on Z.We now give some general remarks about the setting (REF ).Clearly, one motivation for this setting is the case where \Omega 
is a bounded domain in \mathbb {R}^d and Y is one of the spaces H^1(\Omega ),
H_0^1(\Omega ), or C(\bar{\Omega }). Problems of this type will be our
main application in Section 7. Note that REF  is satisfied for
these spaces, cf. {{cite:5349ffcdb3208100915cf224b0d1edd5e5a54bf6}}, {{cite:13b5428afa79705313cf879a66521541cec1915c}} for a proof in H^1.

In theory, we could easily generalize our work by allowing Z to
be an arbitrary Hilbert lattice {{cite:b8dc03b226a5c6f4e5aceb7813665d63b15d15d6}}, {{cite:6fb8a2813a828e163be5291277e2703fce68551c}}, {{cite:877dde016de2a19076b7d2fde7c7b3e331320136}}, {{cite:1dbcd2a416bde9a207323b83adb21c7f7ab0eaed}}. However, it turns out {{cite:6fb8a2813a828e163be5291277e2703fce68551c}} that every
Hilbert lattice is (isometrically and lattice) isomorphic to L^2(\Omega )
for some measure space \Omega . Hence, this seemingly more general setting
is already covered by ours.

Related to the previous point, we note that our setting also covers
the case Y=\mathbb {R}^m, which is a Hilbert lattice and can be identified with
L^2(\Omega ) on the discrete measure space \Omega =\lbrace 1,\ldots ,m\rbrace .We conclude this section by proving a lemma for later reference. Recall that
\left( \cdot ,\cdot  \right)_Z denotes the scalar product in Z=L^2(\Omega ).Lemma 2.2 
Let (a^k) and (b^k) be bounded sequences in Z. Then
\min \lbrace a^k,b^k\rbrace \rightarrow 0 implies \left( a^k,b^k \right)_Z\rightarrow 0.It is easy to see that \left( a^k,b^k \right)_Z=\left( \min \lbrace a^k,b^k\rbrace ,\max \lbrace a^k,b^k\rbrace  \right)_Z. Since \min \lbrace a^k,b^k\rbrace \rightarrow 0 and the sequence (\max \lbrace a^k,b^k\rbrace ) is bounded, it follows that \left( a^k,b^k \right)_Z\rightarrow 0.Note that the above lemma becomes false if we drop the boundedness of one
of the sequences. For instance, consider the case where \Omega =\lbrace 1\rbrace  and
Z=L^2(\Omega ), which can be identified with \mathbb {R}. Then the sequences
a^k=k and b^k=1/k provide a simple counterexample.

An Augmented Lagrangian Method.text:
This section gives a detailed statement of our augmented Lagrangian
method for the solution of the optimization problem (REF ).
It is motivated by the finite-dimensional discussion in, e.g.,
{{cite:2bb4d3bb8ed1e7fcf9f019be0b6c81ed83196451}} and differs from the traditional augmented
Lagrangian method as applied, e.g., in {{cite:98e16c9b56b6025138e508bc39b425f18d947678}}, {{cite:50085ef420cdb0b9926b1f1ab48b609ae7a5eb72}} to a class
of infinite-dimensional problems, in a more controlled
updating of the Lagrange multiplier estimates.We begin by defining the augmented LagrangianL_{\rho }:X\times Z\rightarrow \mathbb {R}, \quad L_{\rho }(x,\lambda ):=
f(x)+\frac{\rho }{2}
\left\Vert \left( g(x)+\frac{\lambda }{\rho } \right)_+\right\Vert _Z^2.This enables us to formulate the following algorithm for the solution of
(REF ), which is a variant of the (finite-dimensional) method from
{{cite:2bb4d3bb8ed1e7fcf9f019be0b6c81ed83196451}} in the context of our optimization problem (REF ).
In fact, formally, the method looks almost identical to the one from
{{cite:2bb4d3bb8ed1e7fcf9f019be0b6c81ed83196451}}, but some of the notations related to the order in Y or Z
have a different and more general meaning than those in the finite-dimensional
literature.Algorithm 3.1 (Augmented Lagrangian method)[font=]
(S.0)
Let (x^0,\lambda ^0)\in X\times Z, \rho _0>0,
w^{\max }\in K_Z, \gamma >1, \tau \in (0,1), and set k=0.
(S.1)
If (x^k,\lambda ^k) satisfies a suitable stopping criterion: STOP.
(S.2)
Choose 0\le w^k\le w^{\max } and compute an approximate
solution x^{k+1} of

\min _{x\in X}\ L_{\rho _k}(x,w^k).

(S.3)
Set \lambda ^{k+1}:=\left(w^k+\rho _k g(x^{k+1})\right)_+.
If k=0 or

\left\Vert \min \left\lbrace -g(x^{k+1}),\frac{w^k}{\rho _k}\right\rbrace \right\Vert _Z
\le \tau \left\Vert \min \left\lbrace -g(x^k),\frac{w^{k-1}}{\rho _{k-1}}
\right\rbrace \right\Vert _Z

holds, set \rho _{k+1}:=\rho _k; otherwise, set \rho _{k+1}:=\gamma \rho _{k}.
(S.4)
Set k\leftarrow k+1 and go to (S.1).Note that the case k=0 is considered separately in Step 3 for
formal reasons only since w^{k-1} and \rho _{k-1} are not defined
for this value of the iteration counter. In any case, the treatment
of this initial step has no influence on our convergence theory.One of the most important aspects of the above algorithm is the sequence (w^k).
Note that w^k\le w^{\max } implies that (w^k) is bounded in Z.
Apart from this boundedness, there is a certain degree of freedom in the choice of
w^k. For instance, we could always choose w^k:=0 and thus obtain
a simplified algorithm which is essentially a quadratic penalty method. Going a
little further, our method also includes the Moreau-Yosida regularization scheme
(see {{cite:fb89da83a293fbcadc88c0b74e4f3f36b60f130d}}, {{cite:bbddb591dafd85fd8abccba19780d1b2ff384976}} and Section ) as a special
case, which arises if (w^k) is chosen as a constant sequence. However, the
most natural choice, which also brings the method closer to traditional augmented
Lagrangian schemes, is w^k:=\min \lbrace \lambda ^k,w^{\max }\rbrace . That is,
w^k is a bounded analogue of the possibly unbounded multiplier \lambda ^k.Another part of Algorithm REF  which needs some explanation is our
notion of an “approximate solution” in Step 2. The reason we have not
specified this part is because we will carry out two distinct convergence
analyses which each require different assumptions.

Global Minimization.text:
We begin by considering Algorithm REF  from a global optimization
perspective. Note that most of the analysis in this section can be carried
out in the more general case where f is an extended real-valued function,
i.e. f maps to  \mathbb {R}\cup \lbrace +\infty \rbrace .The global optimization perspective is particularly valid for convex
problems, where we can expect to solve the subproblems in Step 2 in a
global sense. This is reflected in the following assumption, which we
require throughout this section.Assumption 4.1 
In Step 2 of Algorithm REF , we obtain x^{k+1} such that there
is a sequence \varepsilon _k\downarrow 0 with L_{\rho _k}(x^{k+1},w^k)
\le L_{\rho _k}(x,w^k)+\varepsilon _k for all x\in X and k\in \mathbb {N}.This assumption is quite natural and basically asserts that
we finish each inner iteration with a point that is (globally) optimal within
some tolerance \varepsilon _k, and that this tolerance vanishes asymptotically.Apart from Assumption REF , the main requirement for the following
theorem is the weak lower semicontinuity of f and \Vert g_+\Vert _Z, cf. REF .
Note that \Vert g_+\Vert _Z being weakly lsc implies a slightly stronger statement.
If x^k\rightharpoonup x and z^k\rightarrow 0 in Z, then the nonexpansiveness of z\mapsto z_+
(which is just the projection onto K_Z) together with REF  implies that\liminf _{k\rightarrow \infty }\big \Vert (g(x^k)+z^k)_+\big \Vert _Z=
\liminf _{k\rightarrow \infty }\big \Vert g_+(x^k)\big \Vert _Z \ge \Vert g_+(x)\Vert _Z.This fact will be used in the proof of the following theorem.Theorem 4.2 
Suppose that REF  and Assumption REF  hold. Let (x^k)
be a sequence generated by Algorithm REF , and let \bar{x} be a
weak limit point of (x^k). Then:\bar{x} is a global minimum of the function \Vert g_+(x)\Vert _Z^2.

If \bar{x} is feasible, then \bar{x} is a solution of the
optimization problem (REF ).(a): We first consider the case where (\rho _k) is bounded. Recalling
(REF ), we obtain\Vert g_+(x^{k+1})\Vert _Z\le \left\Vert  \min \left\lbrace  -g(x^{k+1}), \frac{w^k}{\rho _k} \right\rbrace  \right\Vert _Z
\rightarrow 0.Hence REF  implies that \bar{x} is feasible and the assertion
follows trivially.Next, we consider the case where \rho _k\rightarrow \infty . Let \mathcal {K}\subset \mathbb {N}
be such that x^{k+1}\rightharpoonup _{\mathcal {K}}\bar{x} and assume that there is an
x\in X with \Vert g_+(x)\Vert _Z^2<\Vert g_+(\bar{x})\Vert _Z^2.
By (REF ), the boundedness of (w^k), and the fact
that \rho _k\rightarrow \infty , there is a constant c>0 such that\left\Vert \left(g(x^{k+1})+\frac{w^k}{\rho _k}\right)_+\right\Vert _Z^2 >
\left\Vert \left(g(x)+\frac{w^k}{\rho _k}\right)_+\right\Vert _Z^2+cholds for all k\in \mathcal {K} sufficiently large. Hence,L_{\rho _k}(x^{k+1},w^k)>L_{\rho _k}(x,w^k)+\frac{\rho _k c}{2}+f(x^{k+1})-f(x).Using Assumption REF , we arrive at the inequality\varepsilon _k > \frac{\rho _k c}{2}+f(x^{k+1})-f(x),where \varepsilon _k\rightarrow 0. Since (f(x^{k+1}))_{\mathcal {K}} is bounded from
below by the weak lower semicontinuity of f, this is a contradiction.(b): Let \mathcal {K}\subset \mathbb {N} be such that x^{k+1}\rightharpoonup _{\mathcal {K}}\bar{x},
and let x be any other feasible point. From Assumption REF ,
we getL_{\rho _k}(x^{k+1},w^k)\le L_{\rho _k}(x,w^k)+\varepsilon _k.Again, we distinguish two cases. First assume that  \rho _k \rightarrow \infty .
By the definition of the augmented Lagrangian, we have (recall that x
is feasible)f(x^{k+1})\le f(x)+\frac{\rho _k}{2} \left\Vert \left( g(x)+\frac{w^k}{\rho _k}
\right)_+ \right\Vert _Z^2 +\varepsilon _k \le f(x)+\frac{\Vert w^k\Vert _Z^2}{2 \rho _k}+\varepsilon _k.Taking limits in the above inequality, using the boundedness of (w^k)
and the weak lower semicontinuity of f, we get f(\bar{x})\le f(x).Next, consider the case where (\rho _k) is bounded. Using the feasibility
of x and a similar inequality to above, it follows thatf(x^{k+1})+\frac{\rho _k}{2} \left\Vert \left( g(x^{k+1})+
\frac{w^k}{\rho _k} \right)_+ \right\Vert _Z^2 \le f(x)+\frac{\rho _k}{2}\left\Vert \frac{w^k}{\rho _k}\right\Vert _Z^2+\varepsilon _k.But\left( g(x^{k+1})+\frac{w^k}{\rho _k} \right)_+ = \frac{w^k}{\rho _k} -
\min \left\lbrace  -g(x^{k+1}), \frac{w^k}{\rho _k} \right\rbraceand the latter part tends to 0 because of (REF ).
This implies f(\bar{x})\le f(x).Note that, for part (a) of the theorem, we did not fully use \varepsilon _k
\downarrow 0; we only used the fact that (\varepsilon _k) is bounded.
Hence, this result remains true under weaker conditions than those given
in Assumption REF . Furthermore, note that
Theorem REF  does not require any differentiability
assumption, though, in practice, the approximate solution of the subproblems
in (S.2) of Algorithm REF  might be easier under differentiability
assumptions. Finally, note that, in view of statement (a), the weak
limit point  \bar{x}  is always feasible if the feasible set of
the optimization problem (REF ) is nonempty, i.e. in this case
the feasibility assumption from statement (b) is always satisfied.
On the other hand, if the feasible set is empty, it is interesting to
note that statement (a) still holds, whereas the assumption from
statement (b) cannot be satisfied.We now turn to a convergence theorem which guarantees, under certain assumptions,
the (strong) convergence of the whole sequence (x^k). Such an assertion usually
requires a suitable convexity or second-order condition and, in fact, there are
many results along this line in the context of augmented Lagrangian methods,
e.g. {{cite:e58a323da103e90628ac8fa71950d52f054504ea}}, {{cite:55e37466bf0c7575a1cd18781a997b043a020a52}} in finite or {{cite:fb89da83a293fbcadc88c0b74e4f3f36b60f130d}}
in infinite dimensions. Here, we prove a theorem which shows that our method
converges globally for convex problems where the objective function is strongly
convex. Note that, in the convex setting, the lower semicontinuity assumption
REF  is fairly weak since it is always implied by (ordinary) continuity.
Moreover, let us emphasize that the theorem below does not require any Lagrange
multiplier or constraint qualification.Theorem 4.3 
Suppose that REF  and Assumption REF  hold, and that X is
reflexive. Furthermore, assume that g is convex, that f is strongly
convex, and that the feasible set of (REF ) is nonempty. Then (REF )
admits a unique solution \bar{x}, and the sequence (x^k) from
Algorithm REF  converges (strongly) to \bar{x}.Under the given assumptions, it is easy to show that f is coercive and that
the feasible set of (REF ) is closed and convex, hence weakly closed.
Therefore, existence and uniqueness of the solution \bar{x} follow from
standard arguments.Now, denoting by c>0 the modulus of convexity of f, it follows that\frac{c}{8} \Vert x^{k+1}-\bar{x}\Vert _X^2 \le \frac{f(x^{k+1})+f(\bar{x})}{2}-
f( \frac{x^{k+1}+\bar{x}}{2} )for all k. By the proof of Theorem REF  (b), it is easy to
see that \limsup _{k\rightarrow \infty }f(x^{k+1})\le f(\bar{x}). Hence, taking into
account that f is bounded from below, it follows from (REF )
that (x^k) is bounded. Since X is reflexive and every weak limit point
of (x^k) is a solution of (REF ) by Theorem REF ,
we conclude that x^k\rightharpoonup \bar{x}. In particular, the weak lower
semicontinuity of f together with \limsup _{k\rightarrow \infty }f(x^{k+1})\le f(\bar{x})
implies that f(x^{k+1})\rightarrow f(\bar{x}). Moreover, we also have
f(\bar{x})\le \liminf _{k\rightarrow \infty }f\bigl ( (x^k+\bar{x})/2 \bigr ). Hence,
(REF ) implies \Vert x^{k+1}-\bar{x}\Vert _X\rightarrow 0.The above theorem also shows that strong convergence of the primal iterates is not
completely unrealistic, even in infinite dimensions. It may be possible to also prove
strong convergence by using some local condition (e.g. a suitable second-order
sufficient condition in a stationary point). However, we will now explore this
subject any further in the present paper.

Sequential KKT conditions.text:
Throughout this section, we assume that f and g are continuously
Fréchet-differentiable on X, and discuss the KKT conditions of the
optimization problem (REF ). Recalling that K_Y is the nonnegative
cone in Y, we denote byK_Y^+ := \lbrace  f\in Y^* \mid \left\langle f,y \right\rangle \ge 0~
\forall y\in K_Y \rbraceits dual cone. This enables us to define the KKT conditions as follows.Definition 5.1 
A tuple (x,\lambda )\in X\times K_Y^+ is called a KKT point of
(REF ) iff^{\prime }(x)+g^{\prime }(x)^*\lambda =0, \quad g(x)\le 0, \quad \text{and}\quad \left\langle \lambda ,g(x) \right\rangle =0.We also call x\in X a KKT point of (\ref {Eq:Opt}) if
(x,\lambda ) is a KKT point for some \lambda .From a practical perspective, when designing an algorithm for the solution
of (REF ), we will expect the algorithm to generate a sequence which
satisfies the KKT conditions in an asymptotic sense. Hence, it will be
extremely important to discuss a sequential analogue of the KKT conditions.Definition 5.2 
We say that the asymptotic KKT (or AKKT) conditions hold in a feasible
point x\in X if there are sequences x^k\rightarrow x and (\lambda ^k)\subset K_Y^+
such that\quad f^{\prime }(x^k)+g^{\prime }(x^k)^* \lambda ^k\rightarrow 0 \quad \text{and}\quad \left\langle \lambda ^k,g_-(x^k) \right\rangle \rightarrow 0.Asymptotic KKT-type conditions have previously been considered in the
literature {{cite:548c0f928a120a47d9e50d7637f6b6f57874f854}}, {{cite:543e5a863ef4741bb92fa8a415a08e6abe76fd5d}}, {{cite:2bb4d3bb8ed1e7fcf9f019be0b6c81ed83196451}} for
finite-dimensional optimization problems. Furthermore,
in {{cite:2bb4d3bb8ed1e7fcf9f019be0b6c81ed83196451}}, it is shown that AKKT is a necessary
optimality condition even in the absence of constraint qualifications. With
little additional work, this result can be extended to our infinite-dimensional
setting.Theorem 5.3 
Suppose that REF , REF  hold, and that X is reflexive. Then
every local solution \bar{x} of (REF ) satisfies the AKKT conditions.To simplify the proof, we assume that the squared norm q(x):=\Vert x\Vert _X^2 is continuously differentiable on X; since X is reflexive, this is no restriction as X can be renormed equivalently with
a continuously differentiable norm {{cite:e83858c50b16c74790ff5a74ff0933c93124bae4}}, {{cite:77814171425114c50d6e7c94236bf9f88b102e31}}. By assumption, there is an r>0 such that \bar{x} solves (REF ) on B_r(\bar{x}). Now, for k\in \mathbb {N}, consider the problem\min \ f(x)+k\Vert g_+(x)\Vert _Z^2+\Vert x-\bar{x}\Vert _X^2 \quad \text{s.t.}\quad x\in B_r(\bar{x}).Since the above objective function is weakly lsc and B_r(\bar{x}) is weakly
compact, this problem admits a solution x^k. Due to (x^k)\subset B_r(\bar{x}),
there is a \mathcal {K}\subset \mathbb {N} such that x^k\rightharpoonup _{\mathcal {K}}\bar{y}
for some \bar{y}\in B_r(\bar{x}). Since x^k is a solution of
(REF ), we havef(x^k)+k\Vert g_+(x^k)\Vert _Z^2+\Vert x^k-\bar{x}\Vert _X^2 \le f(\bar{x})for every k. Dividing by k and taking the limit k\rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}}\infty ,
we obtain from REF  that \Vert g_+(\bar{y})\Vert _Z=0, i.e. \bar{y} is
feasible. By (REF ), we also obtain
f(\bar{y})+\Vert \bar{y}-\bar{x}\Vert _X^2\le f(\bar{x}). But f(\bar{x})\le f(\bar{y}), hence \bar{x}=\bar{y} and (REF ) implies that x^k\rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}}\bar{x}.
In particular, we have \Vert x^k-\bar{x}\Vert _X<r for sufficiently large
k\in \mathcal {K}, and from (REF ) we obtainf^{\prime }(x^k) + 2 k g^{\prime }(x^k)^* g_+(x^k) + q^{\prime } (x^k-\bar{x})=0.Define \lambda ^k:=2 k g_+(x^k). Then f^{\prime }(x^k)+g^{\prime }(x^k)^*\lambda ^k
\rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}} -q^{\prime }(0)=0 and \left\langle \lambda ^k,g_-(x^k) \right\rangle =0.The above theorem also motivates our definition of the AKKT conditions. In
particular, it justifies the formulation of the complementarity condition as
\left\langle \lambda ^k,g_-(x^k) \right\rangle \rightarrow 0, since the proof shows that (\lambda ^k)
need not be bounded. Hence, the conditions\min \lbrace -g(x^k),\lambda ^k\rbrace \rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}}0, \quad \left\langle \lambda ^k,g(x^k) \right\rangle \rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}}0,
\quad \text{and}\quad \left\langle \lambda ^k,g_-(x^k) \right\rangle \rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}} 0are not equivalent. Note that the second of these conditions (which might
appear as the most natural formulation of the complementarity condition) is
often violated by practical algorithms {{cite:543e5a863ef4741bb92fa8a415a08e6abe76fd5d}}.In order to get the (clearly desirable) implication “AKKT \Rightarrow  KKT”,
we will need a suitable constraint qualification. In the finite-dimensional
setting, constraint qualifications such as MFCQ and
CPLD {{cite:2bb4d3bb8ed1e7fcf9f019be0b6c81ed83196451}}, {{cite:5a9b04321a408e02eab2a3f962b5341cf67af989}}
have been used to enable this transition. However, in the infinite-dimensional
setting, our choice of constraint qualification is much more restricted. For
instance, we are not aware of any infinite-dimensional analogues of the (very
amenable) CPLD condition. Hence, we have decided to employ the Zowe-Kurcyusz
regularity condition {{cite:7902a016243e2c0fa7f2946824165b8291bbe721}}, which is known to be equivalent to the
Robinson condition {{cite:024eab83678ee40860f00068105de9e2f1e2b107}} and to be a generalization of the
finite-dimensional MFCQ. It should be noted, however, that any condition
which guarantees “AKKT \Rightarrow  KKT” could be used in our analysis.Definition 5.4 
The Zowe-Kurcyusz condition holds in a feasible point x\in X ifg^{\prime }(x)X+\operatorname{cone}(K_Y+g(x))=Y,where \operatorname{cone}(K_Y+g(x)) is the conical hull of K_Y+g(x) in Y.We note that the complete theory in this paper can be written down with
 Y = Z  only, so, formally, there seems to be no reason for introducing
the imbedded space  Y . One of the main reasons for the more general
framework considered here with an additional space  Y  is that
suitable constraint qualifications like the above Zowe-Kurcyusz condition
are typically violated even in simple applications when formulated in
 Z , whereas we will see in Section 7 that this condition easily holds in
suitable spaces  Y . We therefore stress the importance of
Definition REF  being defined in  Y , and not in  Z .Let us also remark that the applicability of the Zowe-Kurcyusz condition
very much depends on the particular structure of the constraints. For many
simple constraints, the operator g^{\prime }(x) is actually surjective, which implies
that (REF ) holds trivially. This is the case, for instance,
when dealing with one-sided box constraints in a suitable function space.
(The case of two-sided box constraints is more difficult; see, e.g.,
{{cite:919021e394f914b312ea270ac2289769753c7bbb}}.) Another case where the Zowe-Kurcyusz condition holds
automatically is if K_Y has a nonempty interior and the problem satisfies
a linearized Slater condition, e.g. {{cite:919021e394f914b312ea270ac2289769753c7bbb}}.One of the most important consequences of the Zowe-Kurcyusz condition
is that the set of multipliers corresponding to a KKT point x is bounded
{{cite:7902a016243e2c0fa7f2946824165b8291bbe721}}. From this point of view, it is natural to expect that
the sequence (\lambda ^k) from Definition REF  is bounded,
provided the limit point x satisfies the Zowe-Kurcyusz condition.Theorem 5.5 
Suppose that REF  holds. Let x\in X be a point which satisfies the
AKKT conditions, and let (x^k), (\lambda ^k) be the corresponding sequences
from Definition REF .If x satisfies the Zowe-Kurcyusz condition, then (\lambda ^k)
is bounded in Y^*.

If REF , REF  hold and (\lambda ^k) is bounded
in Y^*, then x is a KKT point.(a): In view of {{cite:7902a016243e2c0fa7f2946824165b8291bbe721}}, the Zowe-Kurcyusz condition
implies that there is an r>0 such thatB_r^Y \subset g^{\prime }(x) B_1^X + (K_Y+g(x)) \cap B_1^Y,where B_r^X and B_r^Y are the closed r-balls around zero in X and Y,
respectively. By the AKKT conditions and REF , there is a
k_0\in \mathbb {N} such that\Vert g(x^k)-g(x)\Vert _Y\le \frac{r}{4}
\quad \text{and}\quad \Vert g^{\prime }(x^k)-g^{\prime }(x)\Vert _{\mathcal {L}(X,Y)}\le \frac{r}{4}for every k\ge k_0. Now, let u\in B_r^Y and k\ge k_0. It follows that
-u=g^{\prime }(x)w+z with \Vert w\Vert _X\le 1 and z=z_1+g(x), \Vert z\Vert _Y\le 1,
z_1\in K_Y. Furthermore, the AKKT conditions imply\left\langle \lambda ^k,z_1+g(x^k) \right\rangle 
& = \left\langle \lambda ^k,z_1 \right\rangle  +\left\langle \lambda ^k,g_+(x^k) \right\rangle  - \left\langle \lambda ^k,g_-(x^k) \right\rangle  \\
& \ge -\left\langle \lambda ^k,g_-(x^k) \right\rangle  \\
& \rightarrow 0,i.e. \left\langle \lambda ^k,z_1+g(x^k) \right\rangle  is bounded from below. Using once again the
AKKT conditions, we see that \left\langle \lambda ^k,g^{\prime }(x^k)w \right\rangle  is also bounded, and
it follows that\left\langle \lambda ^k,u \right\rangle  & = - \left\langle \lambda ^k,g^{\prime }(x)w \right\rangle  - \left\langle \lambda ^k,z_1+g(x) \right\rangle  \\
& \le \frac{r}{4}\Vert \lambda ^k\Vert _{Y^*} - \left\langle \lambda ^k,g^{\prime }(x^k)w \right\rangle  +
\frac{r}{4}\Vert \lambda ^k\Vert _{Y^*} - \left\langle \lambda ^k,z_1+g(x^k) \right\rangle  \\
& \le \frac{r}{2}\Vert \lambda ^k\Vert _{Y^*} + Cfor some constant C>0. We conclude that\Vert \lambda ^k\Vert _{Y^*}=\sup _{\Vert u\Vert \le r}\left\langle \lambda ^k,\frac{1}{r}u \right\rangle \le \frac{1}{r}
\left(C+\frac{r}{2}\Vert \lambda ^k\Vert _{Y^*}\right)and, hence, \Vert \lambda ^k\Vert _{Y^*}\le 2C/r.(b): Since (\lambda ^k) is bounded in Y^* and the unit ball in Y^* is
weak-^* sequentially compact by REF ,
there is a \mathcal {K}\subset \mathbb {N} such that
\lambda ^k\rightharpoonup _{\mathcal {K}}^*\lambda  for some \lambda \in Y^*. Using
\lambda ^k \in K_Y^+ for all k\in \mathbb {N}, it follows that\left\langle \lambda ,y \right\rangle =\lim _{k\in \mathcal {K}}\left\langle \lambda ^k,y \right\rangle \ge 0for every y\in K_Y. In other words, \lambda \in K_Y^+. Hence, taking the
limit in the AKKT conditions and using g_-(x^k)\rightarrow g_{-}(x) = g(x) in Y,
which is a consequence of REF  and the feasibility of  x , we
see that (x,\lambda ) satisfies the KKT conditions.The above theorem is a generalization of a well-known result for the
MFCQ constraint qualification in finite dimensions. Recall that, for
Y=\mathbb {R}^m with the natural ordering, the Zowe-Kurcyusz condition is
equivalent to MFCQ {{cite:7902a016243e2c0fa7f2946824165b8291bbe721}}.

Convergence to KKT Points.text:
We now discuss the convergence properties of Algorithm REF 
from the perspective of KKT points. To this end, we make the following
assumption.Assumption 6.1 
In Step 2 of Algorithm REF , we obtain x^{k+1} such that
L_{\rho _k}^{\prime }(x^{k+1},w^k)\rightarrow 0 as k\rightarrow \infty .The above is a very natural assumption which states that x^{k+1} is an
(approximate) stationary point of the respective subproblem. Note that,
from (REF ), we obtain the following formula for the derivative of
L_{\rho _k} with respect to x:L_{\rho _k}^{\prime }(x^{k+1},w^k)
& = f^{\prime }(x^{k+1})+g^{\prime }(x^{k+1})^* (w^k+\rho _k g(x^{k+1}))_+ \\
& = f^{\prime }(x^{k+1})+g^{\prime }(x^{k+1})^* \lambda ^{k+1}.Our further analysis is split into a discussion of feasibility and optimality.
Regarding the feasibility aspect, note that we can measure the infeasibility
of a point x by means of the function \Vert g_+(x)\Vert _Z^2. By standard projection
theorems, this is a Fréchet-differentiable function and its derivative is
given by D\Vert g_+(x)\Vert _Z^2=2 g^{\prime }(x)^* g_+(x), cf. {{cite:ec4ff414cc400c0bc601f8a04783b4b9e8f7ad22}}. This will be used in the proof of
the following theorem.Theorem 6.2 
Suppose that REF  and Assumption REF  hold. If (x^k) is
generated by Algorithm REF  and \bar{x} is a limit point of (x^k),
then D\Vert g_+(\bar{x})\Vert _Z^2=0.Let \mathcal {K}\subset \mathbb {N} be such that x^{k+1}\rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}} \bar{x}.
If (\rho _k) is bounded, then we can argue as in the proof of Theorem
REF  (a) and conclude that \bar{x} is feasible. Hence,
there is nothing to prove. Now, assume that \rho _k\rightarrow \infty . By
Assumption REF , we havef^{\prime }(x^{k+1})+g^{\prime }(x^{k+1})^* (w^k+\rho _k g(x^{k+1}))_+\rightarrow 0.Dividing by \rho _k and using the boundedness of (w^k) and
(f^{\prime }(x^{k+1}))_{\mathcal {K}}, it follows thatg^{\prime }(x^{k+1})^* g_+(x^{k+1})\rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}} 0.This completes the proof.Similarly to Theorem REF , we remark that the above result
does not fully use the fact that L_{\rho _k}^{\prime }(x^{k+1},w^k)\rightarrow 0 and remains
valid if this sequence is only bounded.We now turn to the optimality of limit points of Algorithm REF .
To this end, recall that Assumption REF  implies thatf^{\prime }(x^{k+1})+g^{\prime }(x^{k+1})^*\lambda ^{k+1}\rightarrow 0,which already suggests that the sequence of tuples (x^k,\lambda ^k) satisfies
AKKT for the optimization problem (REF ). In fact, the only missing
ingredient is the asymptotic complementarity of g and \lambda . We deal
with this issue in two steps. First, we consider the case where (\rho _k) is
bounded. In this case, we even obtain the (exact) KKT conditions without any
further assumptions.Theorem 6.3 
Suppose that REF  and Assumption REF  hold. Let (x^k) be
generated by Algorithm REF  and assume that (\rho _k) is bounded.
If \bar{x} is a limit point of (x^k), then \bar{x} satisfies the KKT conditions of (REF ) with a multiplier in Z.Let \mathcal {K}\subset \mathbb {N} be such that x^{k+1}\rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}} \bar{x}.
Without loss of generality, we assume that \rho _k=\rho _0 for all k. From
Algorithm REF , it follows that (\lambda ^{k+1})_{\mathcal {K}}
is bounded in Z and\min \left\lbrace -g(x^{k+1}),\frac{w^k}{\rho _0}\right\rbrace \rightarrow 0 \quad \text{in}~Z.As in the proof of Theorem REF  (a), this implies
\Vert g_+(x^{k+1})\Vert _Z\rightarrow 0. Furthermore, from Lemma REF , we
get \left( w^k,g(x^{k+1}) \right)_Z\rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}} 0. Using the definition of
\lambda ^{k+1}, we now obtain\left( \lambda ^{k+1},g(x^{k+1}) \right)_Z
& =\rho _0 \left( \left(\frac{w^k}{\rho _0}+g(x^{k+1})\right)_+,g(x^{k+1}) \right)_Z \\
& =\rho _0 \left( \frac{w^k}{\rho _0}-\min \left\lbrace 
-g(x^{k+1}), \frac{w^k}{\rho _0} \right\rbrace , g(x^{k+1}) \right)_Z \\
& \rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}} 0.Since (\lambda ^{k+1})_{\mathcal {K}} is bounded in Z, this also implies
\left( \lambda ^{k+1},g_-(x^{k+1}) \right)_Z\rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}} 0. Hence, recalling
(REF ), the AKKT conditions hold in \bar{x}.
Now, the claim essentially follows from Theorem REF  (b),
the only difference here is that we are working in the Hilbert space
 Z  instead of  Y  or  Y^* , hence the two conditions REF  and
REF  formally required in Theorem REF  (b) are
automatically satisfied in the current Hilbert space situation.Some further remarks about the case of bounded multipliers are due. In
this case, the multiplier sequence (\lambda ^k)_{\mathcal {K}} is also bounded in Z,
and it does not make a difference whether we state the asymptotic
complementarity of g(x^k) and \lambda ^k as\min \lbrace -g(x^k),\lambda ^k\rbrace \rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}}0, \quad \left( \lambda ^k,g(x^k) \right)_Z\rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}}0,
\quad \text{or}\quad \left( \lambda ^k,g_-(x^k) \right)_Z\rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}} 0,cf. the remarks after Theorem REF .
However, this situation changes
if we turn to the case where (\rho _k) is unbounded. Here, it is essential
that we define the asymptotic KKT conditions exactly as we did in Definition
REF .Theorem 6.4 
Suppose that REF , REF  and Assumption REF  hold.
Let (x^k) be generated by Algorithm REF  and let \rho _k\rightarrow \infty .
Then every limit point \bar{x} of (x^k) which is feasible satisfies AKKT
for the optimization problem (REF ).Let \mathcal {K}\subset \mathbb {N} be such that x^{k+1}\rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}}\bar{x}. Recalling (REF ), it suffices to show that\left(\lambda ^{k+1},g_-(x^{k+1})\right)
=\left((w^k+\rho _k g(x^{k+1}))_+,g_-(x^{k+1})\right)\rightarrow _{\mathcal {K}} 0.To this end, let v^k:=(w^k+\rho _k g(x^{k+1}))_+ \cdot g_-(x^{k+1})\in L^1(\Omega ). Since v^k\ge 0, we show that \int _\Omega v^k \rightarrow 0
by using the dominated convergence theorem. Subsequencing if necessary,
we may assume that g(x^{k+1}) converges pointwise to g(\bar{x}) and that
|g(x^{k+1})| is bounded a.e. by an L^2-function for k\in \mathcal {K}
{{cite:ffcc43cc419b7404c8cc4d2738f9cbd9905e933e}}. It follows that v^k is
bounded a.e. by an L^1-function (recall that, if g(x^{k+1})(t)\ge 0, then
v^k(t)=0). Hence, we only need to show that v^k(t)\rightarrow 0 pointwise.
Let t\in \Omega  and distinguish two cases:Case 1. g(\bar{x})(t)<0. In this case, the pointwise convergence
implies that w^k(t)+\rho _k g(x^{k+1})(t)<0 for sufficiently large k and,
hence, v^k(t)=0 for all such k.Case 2. g(\bar{x})(t)=0. Then consider a fixed  k \in \mathcal {K} . If g(x^{k+1})(t)\ge 0, it follows again from the definition
of v^k that v^k(t)=0. On the other hand, if g(x^{k+1})(t)<0, it follows
that v^k(t)\le w^k(t)\cdot |g(x^{k+1})(t)|, and the right-hand side
converges to zero if this subcase occurs infinitely many times.Summarizing these two cases, the pointwise convergence v^k(t)\rightarrow 0
follows immediately. The assertion is therefore a consequence of
the dominated convergence theorem.For a better overview, we now briefly summarize the two previous
convergence theorems. To this end, let (x^k) be the sequence generated by
Algorithm REF  and let \bar{x} be a limit point of (x^k). For the
sake of simplicity, we assume that REF -REF  hold. Then
Theorems REF , REF  and REF 
imply that \bar{x} is a KKT point if eitherthe sequence (\rho _k) is bounded, or

\rho _k\rightarrow \infty , \bar{x} is feasible and the Zowe-Kurcyusz
condition holds in \bar{x}.Hence, for \rho _k\rightarrow \infty , the success of the algorithm crucially
depends on the achievement of feasibility and the regularity of the
constraint function g. Recall that, by Theorem REF ,
the limit point \bar{x} is always a stationary point of the constraint
violation \Vert g_+(x)\Vert _Z^2. Hence, situations in which \bar{x} is infeasible
are rare; in particular, this cannot occur for convex problems (unless, of
course, the feasible set itself is empty).

The Obstacle Bratu Problem.text:
Let us briefly consider the obstacle Bratu problem {{cite:9a2d91fc5900ccd9b7e3279916540a52a488790b}}, {{cite:7910c3a766a8475f81e87b5a2cb29380fe74227b}}, which we simply refer to as Bratu problem. This is a non-quadratic and nonconvex problem which differs from (REF ) in the choice of objective function. To this end, letf(u):=\Vert \nabla u\Vert _{L^2(\Omega )}^2 - \alpha \int _{\Omega } e^{-u(x)} dxfor some fixed \alpha >0. To ensure well-definedness of f, we require \Omega \subseteq \mathbb {R}^2. As before, we set X:=Y:=H_0^1(\Omega ), Z:=L^2(\Omega ) and consider the minimization problem\min \ f(u) \quad \text{s.t.}\quad u\ge \psifor some fixed obstacle \psi \in X; that is, g(u):=\psi -u. Before we proceed, let us first show that the function f is well-defined and satisfies the assumptions REF  and REF .Lemma 7.1 
The function f is well-defined, weakly lsc and continuously Fréchet differentiable from H^1_0(\Omega ) into \mathbb {R}.In the proof we will follow some arguments of {{cite:39fddd446943a0e0e0e2ad3e6d4546dd50fdf18f}}.
It is only necessary to study the mapping u\mapsto \int _{\Omega } e^{u(x)} dx.
The mapping u\mapsto e^{u} maps bounded sets in H^1_0(\Omega ) to bounded sets in L^p(\Omega ) for all p<\infty , see {{cite:322d211ed9fe4bc795e2058be8588ec1ea989d5a}}.
Let (u_n) be a sequence converging weakly to u in H^1_0(\Omega ). By compact embeddings, this sequence
converges strongly to u in L^p(\Omega ) for all p<\infty . After extracting a subsequence if necessary, we have u_n\rightarrow u pointwise
almost everywhere and e^{u_n}\rightharpoonup \tilde{e} in L^p(\Omega ) for all p<\infty .
By a result of Brezis {{cite:cc6f6a6d2db5c1ef07618c9287ea44e090310fce}}, it follows \tilde{e} = e^{u}. This proves the weak lower semicontinuity of f.Let u,h \in H^1_0(\Omega ) be given. Let us writee^{u+h}-e^u-e^uh = \int _0^1 \int _0^1 e^{u+sth}sh^2 \ dt \ ds,which implies\Vert  e^{u+h}-e^u-e^uh\Vert _{L^1(\Omega )} \le \frac{1}{2}\Vert e^{u+|h|}\Vert _{L^2(\Omega )} \Vert h\Vert _{L^4(\Omega )}^2
\le c\Vert e^{u+|h|}\Vert _{L^2(\Omega )} \Vert h\Vert _{H^1(\Omega )}^2.Using the boundedness property of the mapping u\mapsto e^{u} mentioned above, it follows
 \Vert  e^{u+h}-e^u-e^uh\Vert _{L^1(\Omega )} =o(\Vert h\Vert _{H^1(\Omega )}), which implies the Fréchet differentiability of f.Due to the constraint u\ge \psi , the functional f is bounded from below on the feasible set of (REF ).
Together with the lower-semicontinuity result this implies the existence of solutions of the minimization problem (REF ).
Note that this statement is no longer valid if \Omega \subseteq \mathbb {R}^d with d\ge 3.From a theoretical point of view, the Bratu problem is much more difficult
than the obstacle problem from Section REF . While the
constraint function is equally well-behaved, the objective function in
(REF ) is neither quadratic nor convex. Hence, we cannot
apply Theorem REF  or the theory from Section ,
wheras the KKT-like convergence results from Sections 
and  still hold.To analyse how our method behaves in practice, we again considered
\Omega :=(0,1)^2 and implemented the Bratu problem using the same obstacle
and a similar implementation as we did for the standard obstacle problem.
The resulting images are given in Figure REF , and some iteration
numbers are given in Table REF .
{{table:07bdde63-0239-467b-949a-a4e10abff367}}As with the obstacle problem, we observe that both the augmented Lagrangian and Moreau-Yosida regularization methods scale well with increasing dimension, and the augmented Lagrangian method once again holds a certain advantage in terms of iteration numbers and penalty parameters. In fact, the gap between the two methods is slightly bigger than for the standard obstacle problem.
{{figure:fa536ea7-2fe3-4fbb-beb7-f7b6ba634494}}

Optimal Control Problems.text:
We now turn to a class of optimal control problems subject to a semilinear elliptic equation. Let \Omega \subseteq \mathbb {R}^d, d=2,3, be a bounded Lipschitz domain.
The control problem we consider consists of minimizing the functionalJ(y,u):=\frac{1}{2}\Vert y-y_d\Vert _{L^2(\Omega )}^2 + \frac{\alpha }{2}\Vert u\Vert _{L^2(\Omega )}^2subject to y\in H^1_0(\Omega )\cap C(\bar{\Omega }) and u\in L^2(\Omega ) satisfying the
semilinear equation-\Delta y + d(y) = u \quad \text{in } H^1_0(\Omega )^*and the pointwise state constraintsy\ge y_c \quad \text{in } \Omega .Here, \alpha  is a positive parameter, y_d\in L^2(\Omega ), and y_c\in C(\bar{\Omega }) with y_c\le 0 on \partial \Omega  are given functions. The nonlinearity d in the elliptic equation is induced by a function d:\mathbb {R}\rightarrow \mathbb {R}, which is assumed to be continuously differentiable and monotonically increasing.Before we can apply the augmented Lagrangian method to (REF ), we need to formally eliminate the state equation coupling the variables y and u. Due to elliptic regularity results, this equation admits for each control u\in L^2(\Omega ) a uniquely determined weak solution y\in H^1_0(\Omega )\cap C(\bar{\Omega }). Moreover, the mapping u\mapsto y is Fréchet differentiable in this setting {{cite:919021e394f914b312ea270ac2289769753c7bbb}}. Let us denote this mapping by S. Using S, we can eliminate the state equation to obtain an optimization problem with inequality constraints:\min \ J(S(u),u) \quad \text{s.t.}\quad S(u)\ge y_c.We can now apply Algorithm REF  to this problem. The inequality S(u)\ge y_c has to be understood in the sense of C(\bar{\Omega }), which necessitates the choice Y:=C(\bar{\Omega }). Furthermore, we have X:=Z:=L^2(\Omega ). Assuming a linearized Slater condition, one can prove that the Zowe-Kurcyusz condition is fulfilled, and there exists a Lagrange multiplier \lambda \in C(\bar{\Omega })^* to the inequality constraint S(u)\ge y_c, see, e.g., {{cite:919021e394f914b312ea270ac2289769753c7bbb}}.The subproblems generated by Algorithm REF  are unconstrained optimization problems. By reintroducing the state variable y, we can write these subproblems as\min \ J(y,u)+\frac{\rho _k}{2}\left\Vert  \left( y_c-y+\frac{w^k}{\rho _k} \right)_+ \right\Vert ^2
\quad \text{s.t.}\quad y=S(u).Hence, we have transformed (REF ) into a sequence of optimal control problems which include the state equation but not the pointwise constraint (REF ).Let us proceed with some numerical results. As a test problem, we chose an example similar to the one presented in {{cite:fbb9794aba8972c4778592def8c7c5160fc3ef72}}, where \Omega :=(0,1)^2, d(y):=y^3, \alpha :=10^{-3}, andy_c(x):=-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{2}
\min \lbrace  x_1+x_2,1+x_1-x_2,
1-x_1+x_2,2-x_1-x_2\rbrace .Clearly, in this setting, (REF ) and its reformulation (REF ) are nonconvex problems. We solve the subproblems (REF ) with the MATLAB® function fmincon, where the Hessian of the objective is replaced by a semismooth version thereof.
{{table:2088f4bb-f328-4b56-a44a-0f94250407c9}}Table REF  contains the resulting iteration numbers and final penalty parameters for both the augmented Lagrangian and Moreau-Yosida regularization methods. As with the previous examples, both methods scale well with increasing dimension, and the augmented Lagrangian method is more efficient in terms of iteration numbers and penalty parameters.
{{figure:a0dfca96-e3f7-4da3-b8e4-847a799135df}}The state constraint y_c and the results of our method are given in Figure REF . It is interesting to note that the multiplier \bar{\lambda } appears to be much less regular than the optimal control \bar{u} and state \bar{y}. This is not surprising because, due to our construction, we have\bar{u}\in L^2(\Omega ),\quad \bar{y}\in C(\bar{\Omega }),
\quad \text{and}\quad \bar{\lambda }\in C(\bar{\Omega })^*.The latter is well-known to be the space of Radon measures on \bar{\Omega }, which is a superset of L^2(\Omega ). In fact, the convergence data shows that the (discrete) L^2-norm of \bar{\lambda } grows approximately linearly as n increases, possibly even diverging to +\infty , which suggests that the underlying (infinite-dimensional) problem (REF ) does not admit a multiplier in L^2(\Omega ) but only in C(\bar{\Omega })^*.

Final Remarks.text: We have presented an augmented Lagrangian method for the solution of optimization problems in Banach spaces, which is essentially a generalization of the modified augmented Lagrangian method from {{cite:2bb4d3bb8ed1e7fcf9f019be0b6c81ed83196451}}. Furthermore, we have shown how the method can be applied to well-known problem classes, and the corresponding numerical results appear quite promising. In particular, the method appears to be (slightly) more efficient than the well-known Moreau-Yosida regularization scheme, especially with regard to the behavior of the penalty parameter.From a theoretical point of view, the main strength of our method is the ability to deal with very general classes of inequality constraints; in particular, inequality constraints with infinite-dimensional image space. Other notable features include desirable convergence properties for nonsmooth problems, the ability to find KKT points of arbitrary nonlinear (and nonconvex) problems, and a global convergence result which covers many prominent classes of convex problems. We believe the sum of these aspects to be a substantial contribution to the theory of augmented Lagrangian methods.Another key concern in our work is the compatibility of the algorithm with suitable constraint qualifications. To deal with this matter properly, we investigated the well-known Zowe-Kurcyusz regularity condition {{cite:7902a016243e2c0fa7f2946824165b8291bbe721}}, see also Robinson {{cite:024eab83678ee40860f00068105de9e2f1e2b107}}, and showed that this condition can be used to guarantee the boundedness of suitable multiplier sequences corresponding to asymptotic KKT conditions. While the main application of this result is clearly the boundedness of the multiplier sequence generated by the augmented Lagrangian method, we state explicitly that the underlying theory is independent of our specific algorithm. With the understanding that most iterative methods for constrained optimization usually satisfy the KKT conditions in an asymptotic sense, we hope that this aspect of our theory will facilitate similar research into other methods or find applications in other topics.

Acknowledgement.text: The authors would like to thank two anonymous referees for their helpful suggestions in improving the paper.

metadata.authors: Leszek Demkowicz, Jay Gopalakrishnan, Brendan Keith
metadata.title: The DPG-star method
metadata.abstract:
This article introduces the DPG-star (from now on, denoted DPG$^*$) finite
element method. It is a method that is in some sense dual to the discontinuous
Petrov-Galerkin (DPG) method. The DPG methodology can be viewed as a means to
solve an overdetermined discretization of a boundary value problem. In the same
vein, the DPG$^*$ methodology is a means to solve an underdetermined
discretization. These two viewpoints are developed by embedding the same
operator equation into two different saddle-point problems. The analyses of the
two problems have many common elements. Comparison to other methods in the
literature round out the newly garnered perspective. Notably, DPG$^*$ and DPG
methods can be seen as generalizations of $\mathcal{L}\mathcal{L}^\ast$ and
least-squares methods, respectively. A priori error analysis and a posteriori
error control for the DPG$^*$ method are considered in detail. Reports of
several numerical experiments are provided which demonstrate the essential
features of the new method. A notable difference between the results from the
DPG$^*$ and DPG analyses is that the convergence rates of the former are
limited by the regularity of an extraneous Lagrange multiplier variable.

Introduction.text:
The ideal Discontinuous Petrov–Galerkin (DPG)
Method with Optimal Test Functions
{{cite:768bfb9dabbdb3afa77ca940592600eb582a1025}}, {{cite:f2c115d817743ec25df5ceca0261228b19442fbf}} admits three
interpretations {{cite:93ac222f8484d40a5584178e883dbd9d9f21bb0b}}. First, it can be
viewed as a Petrov–Galerkin (PG) discretization in which optimal test functions are computed on the fly. Here, the word
“optimal” refers to the fact that the test functions realize the
supremum in the discrete inf-sup stability condition and, therefore,
the PG discretization automatically inherits the stability of the
continuous method. The DPG method can also be viewed as a minimum
residual method in which the residual is measured in a dual norm
implied by an underlying test norm. Finally, the DPG method can be
viewed also as a mixed method {{cite:2ae6f7b07808277a2b87e857c64b9ce918e5a66b}} wherein one
simultaneously solves for the Riesz representation of the residual
— the so-called error representation function
— and the approximate solution. All three equivalent
interpretations involve the inversion of a Riesz operator on the test
space which, in general, cannot be done exactly and has to be
approximated. This naturally leads to the introduction of an enriched or search test space — having dimension
larger than that of the latent trial space — and a
discretized Riesz operator. In this way, the corresponding practical DPG method retains its three interpretations, although
now with approximate optimal test functions, an approximate residual, and an approximate error representation
function {{cite:4743d923209234c070124e0812d03ce062a627bf}}, {{cite:e2729dda614db727149ab187284affeaca23948c}}, {{cite:acc5381d6fd9c0bd6d9f86eccb37f7045c754694}}.In the DPG method, the word “discontinuous” corresponds to the use
of discontinuous, but conforming, test functions (from broken spaces)
which make the whole methodology computationally efficient. These
broken spaces also naturally lead to (hybridized) interface solution
variables. Broken space formulations provide a foundation for the DPG
methodology and can be developed for any well-posed variational
formulation {{cite:acc5381d6fd9c0bd6d9f86eccb37f7045c754694}}.Originally motivated by the duality theory in {{cite:2cca4fc71f67787cedcc912e62fa1b2700a59592}}, in
this article, the DPG methodology is expanded on by reconsidering how
a given operator equation can be embedded into a DPG-type saddle-point
problem. In turn, the minimum residual principle underpinning DPG
methods can be discarded for a minimum norm principle and a dual class
of methods (i.e. DPG* methodsDPG* methods are distinct from
the saddle point least squares methods {{cite:5bc9d4390192357a9314eb9ce8ff9faa0cae6d75}} which have
separately been contenders for being named “dual” to DPG methods.) can be
introduced.
Ultimately, an entire class of stable DPG-type mixed methods can be proposed, simply by changing loads in the saddle-point problem and the interpretation of the corresponding solution variables.
This broad perspective can help relate several different methods, including weakly conforming least squares methods {{cite:1160072e4435734c6885821943329d1557aae8f3}} and \mathcal {L}\mathcal {L}^\ast  methods {{cite:b2a4a38a73a385a900ed9047a2ccb60d3704c500}} to the existing DPG theory.This article provides a number of important a priori error
analysis results for DPG* methods.
Unlike standard DPG methods, the convergence rate of a DPG* solution
is not controlled solely by the regularity of the solution itself, but
instead also by the regularity of a Lagrange multiplier variable found
in the corresponding saddle-point formulation. This article also
expands on the recent a posteriori error estimation theory
first introduced in {{cite:2cca4fc71f67787cedcc912e62fa1b2700a59592}} and re-establishes much of
Repin, Sauter, and Smolianski's abstract a posteriori theory
for mixed methods {{cite:cd607745663f6a51d18bd194aaf629794dfdfc86}} in the present context. In
addition, it includes several standard numerical examples to verify
the theory for DPG* methods, including one example employing
hp-adaptive mesh refinement. This work is part of the PhD thesis
{{cite:0e864403e274a5c45b454dc53d9f15e74d651ffb}}.

Forms and discretization.text:
It is traditional to write mixed systems
using a bilinear form defined byb(\mu , \nu ) = \langle { {B}\mu , \nu } \rangle _{V}for all \mu \in {U}, \nu \in {V}. In terms of b,
the mixed problem [eq:Mixedgeneral]eq:Mixedgeneral is to
find v \in {V} and w \in {U} satisfying\left\lbrace 
\begin{}{5}
&(v, \nu )_{V}+
b(w, \nu ) &&
= F(\nu )\,,\quad && \forall \, \nu \in {V},
\\
&b(\mu , v) &&= G(\mu )\,,\quad &&
\forall \, \mu \in {U}.
\end{}
\right.Suppose b arises from a weak formulation of a PDE on a domain
\operatorname{\subseteq }\mathbb {R}^d, which is partitioned into a mesh _h of
finitely many open connected elements K with Lipschitz boundaries
\partial K, such that \hspace{1.94443pt}\overline{\hspace{-1.94443pt}\hspace{-0.83328pt}}\hspace{0.83328pt} is the union of
the closures of all mesh elements K in _h. In this scenario,

Related methods.text:
Let {V}= H(\mathcal {L}_h^\ast ).
For any F\in H(\mathcal {L}_h^\ast )^\prime , the ultraweak DPG formulation defined by eq:1uw can be restated as the following system of variational equations:\left\lbrace 
\begin{}{5}
& (\varepsilon , \nu )_{V}\;+\; (u, \mathcal {L}_h^\ast \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }+ \langle { p,\nu } \rangle _h &&=
F(\nu )\,,
\quad && \forall \, \nu \in H(\mathcal {L}_h^\ast ),
\\
& (\mu , \mathcal {L}_h^\ast \varepsilon )_{\scriptscriptstyle }&&=
0\,,
\quad && \forall \, \mu \in L^2,
\\
& \langle { \rho ,\varepsilon } \rangle _h &&=
0\,,
\quad && \forall \, \rho \in Q(\mathcal {L}_h^\ast ).
\end{}
\right.Likewise, letting {V}= H(\mathcal {L}_h), an ultraweak DPG formulation corresponding to eq:1uw may be defined for any G = G_\times G_h\in (L^2\times Q(\mathcal {L}_h))^\prime :\left\lbrace 
\begin{}{5}
& (v, \nu )_{V}\;-\; (\lambda , \mathcal {L}_h \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }- \langle { \sigma ,\nu } \rangle _h &&=
0\,,
\quad && \forall \, \nu \in H(\mathcal {L}_h),
\\
& (\mu , \mathcal {L}_h v)_{\scriptscriptstyle }&&=
G_(\mu )\,,
\quad && \forall \, \mu \in L^2,
\\
& \langle { \rho ,v } \rangle _h &&=
G_h(\rho )\,,
\quad && \forall \, \rho \in Q(\mathcal {L}_h).
\end{}
\right.Both of the formulations defined above relate to the primal problem
eq:bvp with u=v. Clearly, the role of \mathcal {L}_h and
\mathcal {L}_h^\ast  can be interchanged if a solution of the dual problem
eq:bvp* is of interest.The link between DPG and least-squares methods is well established in
the literature (see e.g. {{cite:8178d53b48fab3916801e77d82ff66a2f41ab9dc}}). DPG* methods, as
it turns out, can be readily identified with the category of so-called
\mathcal {L}\mathcal {L}^\ast  methods {{cite:b2a4a38a73a385a900ed9047a2ccb60d3704c500}}. In this subsection, we
briefly illustrate this and a couple of other notable relationships in
the context of the mixed problems introduced in
sub:operatorequations.

Least-squares methods.text:
Let {V}= L^2 and {U}= H_0(\mathcal {L}).
It is well-known that least-squares finite element methods {{cite:5fc1201bbb6af6ed8a532f9a8eb32b869e02aaf3}} follow from the following saddle-point formulation (cf. eq:dpgA,eq:DPGformulationExpanded):\left\lbrace 
\begin{}{5}
&(\varepsilon , \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }+ (\mathcal {L}u,\nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }&&= F(\nu )\,,\quad &&\forall \, \nu \in L^2\,, \\
&(\mathcal {L}\mu ,\varepsilon )_{\scriptscriptstyle }&&= 0\,,\quad &&\forall \, \mu \in H_0(\mathcal {L})\,.
\end{}
\right.This may be identified with a mixed problem akin to eq:dpgA using the strong formulation of eq:bvp, rather than the ultraweak formulation, as in eq:DPGformulationExpanded.
Indeed, let \operatorname{{R}}_{L^2} be the L^2 Riesz operator appearing in each term in eq:LeastSquares and recall identity eq:normalequation, where ({B}\mu )(\cdot ) = (\mathcal {L}\mu ,\cdot )_{\scriptscriptstyle }.
Then observe that {B}^\prime \operatorname{{R}}_{V}^{\raisebox {.2ex}{\scriptscriptstyle -1}}{B}= (\operatorname{{R}}_{L^2}\mathcal {L})^\prime \operatorname{{R}}_{L^2}^{\raisebox {.2ex}{\scriptscriptstyle -1}}(\operatorname{{R}}_{L^2}\mathcal {L}) = \mathcal {L}^\prime \operatorname{{R}}_{L^2}\mathcal {L} and {B}^\prime \operatorname{{R}}_{V}^{\raisebox {.2ex}{\scriptscriptstyle -1}}F = \mathcal {L}^\prime F.
That is,\langle {B}^\prime \operatorname{{R}}_{V}^{\raisebox {.2ex}{\scriptscriptstyle -1}}{B}u,\mu \rangle _{U}=
\langle {B}^\prime \operatorname{{R}}_{V}^{\raisebox {.2ex}{\scriptscriptstyle -1}}F,\mu \rangle _{U}\qquad \iff \qquad (\mathcal {L}u,\mathcal {L}\mu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }=
F(\mathcal {L}\mu )
\,.In the case F(\cdot ) = (f,\cdot )_{\scriptscriptstyle }, observe that F(\mathcal {L}\nu ) = (f,\mathcal {L}\nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }.
Therefore, the variational equation above can be readily identified with the first-order optimality condition for the functional \mathcal {J}:u\mapsto \Vert \mathcal {L}u-f\Vert _{L^2}^2, \partial _u\mathcal {J}= 0.

null.text:
Let {V}= L^2 and {U}= H_0(\mathcal {L}^\ast ).
Contrary to eq:LeastSquares, so-called \mathcal {L}\mathcal {L}^\ast  methods {{cite:b2a4a38a73a385a900ed9047a2ccb60d3704c500}} relate to the following system (cf. eq:dpg*A,eq:DPG*formulationExpanded):\left\lbrace 
\begin{}{5}
&(v,\nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }- (\mathcal {L}^\ast \lambda ,\nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }&&= 0\,,\quad &&\forall \, \nu \in L^2\,, \\
&(\mathcal {L}^\ast \mu ,v)_{\scriptscriptstyle }&&= G(\mu )\,,\quad &&\forall \, \mu \in H_0(\mathcal {L}^\ast )\,.
\end{}
\right.Likewise, consider eq:normalequation2, where ({B}\mu )(\cdot ) = (\mathcal {L}^\ast \mu ,\cdot )_{\scriptscriptstyle } and G(\cdot ) = (f,\cdot )_{\scriptscriptstyle }.
In this case, we see that \mathcal {L}\mathcal {L}^\ast  formulations may again be identified with eq:bvp, in this case using a saddle-point expression akin to eq:dpg*A.
Indeed, observe that\langle {B}^\prime \operatorname{{R}}_{V}^{\raisebox {.2ex}{\scriptscriptstyle -1}}{B}\lambda ,\mu \rangle _{U}=
\langle G,\mu \rangle _{U}\qquad \iff \qquad (\mathcal {L}^\ast \lambda ,\mathcal {L}^\ast \mu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }=
(f,\mu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }\,.The variational equation above indicates, in a weak sense, that \mathcal {L}\mathcal {L}^\ast \lambda = f.
Recalling that the solution is determined by the transformation v= \operatorname{{R}}_{V}^{\raisebox {.2ex}{\scriptscriptstyle -1}}{B}\lambda = \mathcal {L}^\ast \lambda , we have \mathcal {L}v= f weakly, as well.

Weakly conforming least-squares methods.text:
A weakly conforming least squares method {{cite:1160072e4435734c6885821943329d1557aae8f3}} for the primal problem [eq:bvp]eq:bvp seeks a minimizer of the least squares functionalw\mapsto \Vert \mathcal {L}w- f \Vert ^2_{L^2}\, ,under the conformity constraint\langle w, \rho \rangle _h = 0\,, \quad \forall \, \rho \in Q(\mathcal {L}_h)
\,.Here, of course, the operator \mathcal {L} is understood element-wise so we may saliently replace it by \mathcal {L}_h.
This leads to the following saddle-point problem for the two solution components w and \sigma :\left\lbrace 
\begin{}{5}
&(\mathcal {L}_hw, \mathcal {L}_h \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }+ \langle \sigma , \nu \rangle _h &&= (f, \mathcal {L}_h \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }\,,\quad &&\forall \, \nu \in H(\mathcal {L}_h)\,, \\
&\langle w, \rho \rangle _h &&= 0\,,\quad &&\forall \, \rho \in Q(\mathcal {L}_h)\,.
\end{}
\right.If we use an ultraweak DPG* formulation eq:DPG*formulationExpanded with its corresponding graph inner product eq:GraphInnerProducts, scaled by an arbitrary constant \alpha >0, we arrive at\left\lbrace 
\begin{}{5}
&(\mathcal {L}_h v,\mathcal {L}_h \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }+ \alpha ( v,\nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }- (\lambda ,\mathcal {L}_h\nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }- \langle \sigma ,\nu \rangle _h &&= 0\,,\quad && \forall \, \nu \in H(\mathcal {L}_h)\,, \\
&(\mu , \mathcal {L}_h v)_{\scriptscriptstyle }&&= ( f, \mu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }\,,\quad && \forall \, \mu \in L^2\,, \\
&\langle v, \rho \rangle _h &&= 0\,,\quad && \forall \, \rho \in Q(\mathcal {L}_h)\,.
\end{}
\right.From the second equation in eq:DPG*ultraweak, observe that f = \mathcal {L}_h v.
Therefore, the first equation can be rewritten as(f-\lambda ,\mathcal {L}_h \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }+ \alpha ( v,\nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }= \langle \sigma ,\nu \rangle _h \,,\quad \forall \, \nu \in H(\mathcal {L}_h)\,.Testing only with \nu \in H(\mathcal {L}), so that the term \langle \sigma ,\nu \rangle _h vanishes, it can now be seen that \lambda \rightarrow f as \alpha \rightarrow 0.
Consequently, this particular DPG* formulation can be viewed as a regularization of the weakly conforming least-squares formulation eq:WeaklyConformingLeastSquares.

Solving the primal and dual problems sim.text:
In eq:Mixedgeneral, we may hypothetically consider any F\in {V}^\prime  and G\in {U}^\prime  we wish:\left\lbrace 
\begin{}{3}
\operatorname{{R}}_{V}&v+ {B}w &&= F \,, \\
{B}^\prime &v&&= G \, .
\end{}
\right.Let {B} to be an isomorphism and define F = \operatorname{{R}}_{V}({B}^\prime )^{\raisebox {.2ex}{\scriptscriptstyle -1}}G + \ell , for some fixed \ell \in (\mathrm {Null}\,{B}^\prime )^\perp = {V}^\prime .In the case of an injective but not surjective {B}, consider F = {B}({B}^\prime \operatorname{{R}}_{V}^{\raisebox {.2ex}{\scriptscriptstyle -1}}{B})^{\raisebox {.2ex}{\scriptscriptstyle -1}}G + \ell \in (\mathrm {Null}\,{B}^\prime )^\perp \subsetneq {V}^\prime .
Noting that v= ({B}^\prime )^{\raisebox {.2ex}{\scriptscriptstyle -1}}G, by the second equation in eq:Mixedgeneral2, it is readily seen that {B}w = \ell .
Therefore, with this choice of loads, w=u solves the primal problem eq:Au=f and v solves the dual problem eq:adjointproblem, simultaneously.Introducing the load F, as proposed above, involves the inversion the linear operator {B}^\prime .
In practice, this is usually not feasible and, therefore, precludes the construction of any such load in most circumstances.
Nevertheless, consider the following system of equations:\left\lbrace 
\begin{}{5}
&(\mathcal {L}^\ast v,\mathcal {L}^\ast \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }+ ( w,\mathcal {L}^\ast \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }&&= (g,\mathcal {L}^\ast \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }+ (f,\nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }\,,\quad && \forall \, \nu \in H(\mathcal {L}^\ast )\,, \\
&(\mathcal {L}^\ast v, \mu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }&&= (g,\mu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }\,,\quad && \forall \, \mu \in L^2\,.
\end{}
\right.This corresponds to a system like eq:Mixedgeneral2 with {V}= H(\mathcal {L}^\ast ) and {U}= L^2.
In eq:PrimalDualDPG,  v clearly satisfies (\mathcal {L}^\ast v, \mu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }= ( g, \mu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }.
That is,  v solves the dual problem eq:bvp*, \mathcal {L}^\ast v = g, in a strong sense.
Substituting \mu = \mathcal {L}^\ast \nu  into eq:PrimalDualDPG and canceling terms in the first equation, we immediately find that ( w,\mathcal {L}^\ast \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }= (f,\nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }.
That is, w=u solves the primal problem eq:bvp, \mathcal {L}u = f, in the ultraweak sense.To avoid solving the mixed problem for both  v and w at the same time, upon discretization, broken test spaces spaces can be used.
In this setting, we must consider the following related system with solution ( w,\sigma )\in {U}= L^2\times Q(\mathcal {L}^\ast _h) and  v\in {V}= H(\mathcal {L}^\ast _h):\left\lbrace 
\begin{}{5}
&(\mathcal {L}_h^\ast v,\mathcal {L}_h^\ast \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }+ \alpha ( v,\nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }+ ( w,\mathcal {L}_h^\ast \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }+ \langle \sigma ,\nu \rangle _h &&= (g,\mathcal {L}_h^\ast \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }+ (f,\nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }\,,\quad \!\! && \forall \, \nu \in H(\mathcal {L}^\ast _h), \\
&(\mathcal {L}_h^\ast v, \mu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }&&= (g,\mu )_{\scriptscriptstyle },\quad && \forall \, \mu \in L^2, \\
&\langle v, \rho \rangle _h &&= 0,\quad && \forall \, \rho \in Q(\mathcal {L}^\ast _h).
\end{}
\right.The consequent manipulations are inspired by {{cite:700247ddb0bb7495da9e1566aee1c608c133c724}}.
First, notice that the last two equations in eq:PrimalDualDPGbroken uniquely determine  v.
Therefore, after testing the middle equation with \mu = \mathcal {L}_h^\ast \nu , observe that the first equation can be rewritten( w,\mathcal {L}_h^\ast \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }+ \langle \sigma ,\nu \rangle _h
=
(f,\nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }- \alpha ( v,\nu )
\,.By linearity, ( w,\sigma )_{\scriptscriptstyle }= ( u,q)_{\scriptscriptstyle }+ \alpha (e,r), where ( u,q)\in {U} solves the ultraweak primal problem ( u,\mathcal {L}_h^\ast \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }+ \langle q,\nu \rangle _h = (f,\nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle } (cf. eq:bvp) and (e,r) = (e(v),r(v)) is a pollution term defined by the equation (e,\mathcal {L}_h^\ast \nu )_{\scriptscriptstyle }+ \langle r,\nu \rangle _h = -( v,\nu ).
Clearly,  w\rightarrow u as \alpha \rightarrow 0.

A posteriori error control.text:
In this section, we will present an abstract a posteriori error
estimator valid for all ultraweak DPG* formulations (see
sub:ultraweakformulations). We then proceed to work out the
example of the Poisson problem in full detail. Note that abstract
ultraweak formulations encompass many physical models besides the
Poisson example given above. Other important examples with similar functional settings include convection-dominated diffusion {{cite:a6e552af3d15cc51970527e60c9991c048811123}}, {{cite:78e76c26a842f6be4b5574837144e9601b6780d6}}, Stokes flow
{{cite:d3e6638d32b6c2ea1956acae36f1258cd6fa2c83}}, {{cite:dcd6d639780da30004b90f61e064d0752b6b5b4c}}, linear elasticity
{{cite:05d3eedbae2b8e8c7b84c4b924e34e69591bdf5c}}, {{cite:5bb9e436abe6bc3871546cd284da519c5d8525b8}}, and acoustics
{{cite:d9fc1a7ae19f43316e755519b5e48ac4dfa191b9}}, {{cite:331bbdcab88b256b3626baa725f54d3e42d02377}}, {{cite:5963816b0782f675793214f8fabecba05f780369}}.In this section, we will present an abstract a posteriori error

Numerical experiments.text:
In order to verify the mathematical theory developed above, we conducted several standard numerical verification experiments using two finite element software packages which have been used extensively for implementing DPG methods.
In our first set of experiments, we used Camellia {{cite:c76c60eb184b18d882f4dea375fefa70f4aecd61}}, {{cite:975205d81072a7acf4cbd11c9050b6e8f5ca8b56}}, a user-friendly C++ toolbox developed by Nathan V. Pure Dirichlet boundary conditions on a.text:
Recall eq:ModelProblem.
In this first example, = _\square  and _{\protect \scalebox {0.6}{\mathrm {D}}}= \partial .
We considered two seemingly benign cases for the loads: (i) f=2\pi ^2\sin (\pi x)\sin (\pi y) and v_0 = 0; and (ii) f=0 and v_0 = 1.

\end{aligned}
\right.where g = v - 2\Delta v + \Delta ^2 v.

fig:hUnifSinB presents the convergence of only the solution variable v_h, measured in the L^2()-norm.

metadata.abstract:
We prove a quenched invariance principle for a class of random walks in
random environment on $\mathbb{Z}^d$, where the walker alters its own
environment. The environment consists of an outgoing edge from each vertex. The
walker updates the edge $e$ at its current location to a new random edge $e'$
(whose law depends on $e$) and then steps to the other endpoint of $e'$. We
show that a native environment for these walks (i.e., an environment that is
stationary in time from the perspective of the walker) consists of the wired
uniform spanning forest oriented toward the walker, plus an independent
outgoing edge from the walker.
