A random environment altered by the walk.text:
Label each site of \mathbb {Z}^2 with either `H' or `V'. A walker starts at the origin. At each discrete time step the walker resamples the label at its current location (changing `H' to `V' and `V' to `H' with probability q, independent of the past) and then takes a mean zero horizontal step if the new label is `H' and a mean zero vertical step if the new label is `V'. We do not know how to determine whether such a walk is recurrent or transient! Nevertheless, we will show (see Theorem REF  below) for a certain distribution on initial labels, the scaling limit of the walk is a standard planar Brownian motion.The walk just described is an example of a random walk with local memory: each site of \mathbb {Z}^2 stores one bit of information in its label. For each vertex x that the walk visits, the label of x remembers whether the most recently traversed outgoing edge from x was horizontal or vertical. This memory in turn affects the distribution of the edge traversed the next time the walker returns to x. One can consider more complicated forms of local memory (e.g., that remember several past visits) but they all essentially reduce to a standard retrospective form in which each vertex x is labeled by an outgoing edge from x. At each discrete time step, the walker updates the label e of its current location to a new random edge e^{\prime } (whose law depends on e) and then steps to the other endpoint of e^{\prime }.Pinsky and Travers {{cite:b3592710ef31b4147b0709768c1b828e7e998d68}} and Kosygina and Peterson {{cite:49334da3d3d840fc7a56349851ca843ef9151477}} study random walks with local memory in one dimension under the name “Markovian cookie stacks”, which generalize excited random walks with periodic cookies {{cite:334d097c37a410088bee9d0a20eb4e3f7f564312}}, {{cite:4d3cebe78eb2c13f61a4f241182bcc289e11b391}}.
In particular, the latter characterize when such a walk is recurrent, transient non-ballistic, or ballistic;
and they derive a central limit theorem for each of those cases.
The methods used in {{cite:49334da3d3d840fc7a56349851ca843ef9151477}} are based on the Ray-Knight theorem, and hence are limited only to one dimension.
The aim of this paper is to begin the study of these walks in higher dimensions, by identifying a native environment and proving an invariance principle.In analyzing random walks with local memory in higher dimensions, we take our inspiration from the theory of random walk in random environment {{cite:e90d36da0f63598c8f0ad58ca684ed5fcb4958e1}}, {{cite:09470ad92363bfdac3f2ab8cf648fda008848965}}, in which the environment affects the motion of the walker but the walker does not affect the environment. In our walks, a new difficulty is that the walker alters its own environment.An interesting feature of random walk with local memory is that the walker organizes its environment to form a tree. Indeed, when the walk is expressed in retrospective form, the local state at each previously visited vertex is the last exit edge, so the edges at visited vertices form a tree oriented toward the walker. From this observation, it is natural to use the wired uniform spanning forest (\mathsf {WUSF}) to construct a native environment (i.e., an environment stationary in time from the perspective of the walker; see Section ).The wired uniform spanning forest is defined as follows.
Let W_1\subseteq W_2 \subseteq \ldots  be finite connected subsets of V(G) such that \bigcup _{n=1}^\infty W_n=V(G).
Let G_n be obtained from G by identifying all vertices outside W_n to one new vertex, and let \mu _n be the uniform measure on spanning trees of G_n.
The wired uniform spanning forest is then the unique infinite-volume limit of \mu _n {{cite:0f3a8ee40e6f2601feeb0ece2088c69efe2a980f}}.To build a native environment for the random walk with local memory, we orient the connected component of the origin in the \mathsf {WUSF} toward the origin, orient all other components toward infinity, and add an independent outgoing edge from the origin.
Note that there might be more than one way to orient a component toward infinity if it has more than one end;
we will orient them using the orientation given by Wilson's method rooted toward infinity {{cite:24e6472207dc4b400026dfb5e39f3108927164ad}}.
We denote by {{\mathsf {WUSF}}^+ the oriented subgraph constructed this way.
}The environment given by {{\mathsf {WUSF}}^+ turns out to be a native environment if G is a Cayley graph and the random walk with local memory
is {transitive} and {uniform}.
Here \emph {transitive} means that every vertex follows the same rule in updating their local memory,
and \emph {uniform} means that, averaging over all initial labels, every outgoing edge of the current location is equally likely to be the next label.
}\begin{}
Consider any random walk with local memory on a simple Cayley graph that is transitive and uniform.
Suppose that the initial environment is given by {{\mathsf {WUSF}}^+.
Then, for any n\ge 0,
the environment at the n-th step of the walk {viewed from the perspective of the walker} also follows the law of {{\mathsf {WUSF}}^+.
}
}We prove Theorem~\ref {theorem: intro stationarity} by proving an analogous statement for finite graphs, and then passing to a limit.
See Theorem~\ref {stationarity theorem} for a more general version that does not require the uniform assumption.
\end{}In the case when G is the integer lattice \mathbb {Z}^d (d
\ge 1)
and the random walk with local memory is a martingale and is elliptic,
we can prove an almost sure invariance principle.
Here a martingale means that,
conditioned on the present location,
the expected next location of the walker is equal to the present location;
and elliptic means that, at any step of the walk,
any neighbor of the current location is visited next with positive probability.Theorem 1.1 
Consider any random walk with local memory on \mathbb {Z}^d that is uniform, elliptic, and a martingale.
Then, for almost every environment picked from {{\mathsf {WUSF}}^+,
the trajectory of the walker scales to the standard Brownian motion in \mathbb {R}^d.
That is to say,
 \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} ({X_{\lfloor nt \rfloor }})_{t \ge 0} \overset{ n \rightarrow \infty }{ \Longrightarrow } B(t).
Here X_{\lfloor nt \rfloor } is the location of the walker at the \lfloor nt \rfloor -th step of the walk,
B(t) is standard Brownian motion in \mathbb {R}^d,
and the convergence is weak convergence in the Skorohod space D_{\mathbb {R}^d}[0,\infty ).
}
See Theorem  in Section  for a more general version of this theorem that does not require the uniform assumption.Our proof of Theorem REF  uses the usual tools of random walks in random environments,
namely the martingale CLT and the pointwise ergodic theorem.
We illustrate the flavor with the `H,V'-walk described above (with q strictly between 0 and 1). By the martingale CLT,
the problem reduces to showing that the
walker encounters the label `V' half of the time, i.e.,\frac{1}{n} \sum _{i=0}^{n-1} \mathbb {1}\lbrace \text{the label used by the walker at the $i$-th step is `V'}\rbrace  \longrightarrow \frac{1}{2},in probability as n \rightarrow \infty .
The convergence in equation (REF ) in turn follows from the pointwise ergodic theorem.
Note that, in order to apply the pointwise ergodic theorem,
we need the show that the environment picked from {{\mathsf {WUSF}}^+ is native and ergodic.
The former follows from Theorem~\ref {theorem: intro stationarity} while the latter is derived from the tail triviality of the wired spanning forest.
}

Related work.text:
When each vertex uses a deterministic rule to update its local memory,
the random walk with local memory is known as rotor walk{{cite:7f4b653c581e259126a32f226c6a9bdef8206e20}}, {{cite:ab835365d958abdfa25f8b8332ff2e094461f4b8}}, {{cite:a2a03e9342a6a478e53f8563511a882fb41a7615}}.
That is to say, each vertex is given a prescribed cyclic ordering on its outgoing edges,
and for every update the vertex changes the current edge to the next edge in the cyclic order.
A fundamental difficulty with rotor walk is its lack of randomness:
For example, it is an open problem to prove that the rotor walk in \mathbb {Z}^2 with i.i.d. uniform initial rotors is recurrent; see {{cite:3557cbe6fb2accbedd7d02c704f339dd2d229799}}, {{cite:6e15cc63ea41e8a3758547552060c99fa8a4476f}} for an exposition of this and related problems.Excited random walk {{cite:4cbff857aa88076b0783873a47629d5f9f3d7a3c}} is a variant of random walk with local memory in which the next label of each vertex does not depend on the current label, and instead is predetermined at the beginning of the walk.
We refer to {{cite:ce22f4c683db9f5f094f75d8d19d0e59a630046c}} for a survey of this topic.Random walks with local memory is a special case of stochastic abelian network {{cite:e2b07e5539f0e0f8b066a806549a174cab389e46}},
in which walkers might be added or removed at every step depending on the current environment of the walk.The main motivation of this paper is to begin extending the results of {{cite:49334da3d3d840fc7a56349851ca843ef9151477}}, {{cite:0fb82fa6e30a9b020cae4b37fdad4dbc4d30a747}} from dimension one to higher dimensions, which we partly achieve in Theorem REF .
In particular, it is shown in {{cite:0fb82fa6e30a9b020cae4b37fdad4dbc4d30a747}} that the scaling limit for p-rotor walk in \mathbb {Z}
(where the next edge points in the same direction as the current edge with probability p, and points in the opposite direction with probability 1-p)
is a perturbed Brownian motion.
This perturbation is caused by the initial environment in {{cite:0fb82fa6e30a9b020cae4b37fdad4dbc4d30a747}} not being a native environment.
We expect that proving a scaling limit
for any higher-dimensional random walk with local memory in a non-native environment
will require major new ideas (for example, what are the planar and higher-dimensional analogues of the one-dimensional “Brownian motion perturbed at extrema”?).

Outline.text:
Section  contains the precise definition of our walks with local memory.
Certain walks with local memory admit a routine application of the martingale CLT, regardless of initial environment. We treat these first in Section .In Section  we show the reduction that converts random walks with more complicated forms of local memory to the the standard retrospective form, at the cost of
changing the underlying graph to a larger graph that might has multiple edges.In Section  we construct the wired spanning forest oriented toward a fixed vertex, which is a simple modification of the construction in {{cite:24e6472207dc4b400026dfb5e39f3108927164ad}}. This section applies to any electrical network.In Section  we use the oriented wired spanning forest from Section  to construct a native environment for random walk with local memory. This section applies to any weighted Cayley graph.In Section  we restrict to lattice subgraphs of \mathbb {R}^d, and prove an almost sure invariance principle (weak convergence to Brownian motion) for certain random walks with local memory.We conclude in Section  with a list of open problems.

Random walks with local memory.text:
Throughout this paper G:=(V(G),E(G)) denotes a connected, undirected graph that is locally finite (every vertex has finite degree) and simple (no loops, no multiple edges), with the exception of Section  where a graph may have multiple edges.
When the graph G is evident from context, we will omit G from the notation and write V and E instead.A neighbor of a vertex x is a vertex y such that \lbrace x,y\rbrace  \in E. We denote by {N}(x) the set of all neighbors of x.
An oriented edge of G is a pair (x,y) \in V \times V such that \lbrace x,y\rbrace  is an (unoriented) edge of G.
We call (x,y) an outgoing edge of x and an incoming edge of y.
In an oriented subgraph of G,
the outdegree (respectively, indegree) of x is the number of outgoing (respectively, incoming) edges of x in the oriented subgraph.
We denote by {{E} the set of oriented edges of G.
}The running example for a graph in this paper is the integer lattice \mathbb {Z}^d of dimension d, i.e., the graph given byV&:=\lbrace  \mathbf {x}\mid \mathbf {x}\in \mathbb {Z}^d \rbrace ; \qquad {E}:=\lbrace  \lbrace \mathbf {x}, \mathbf {y}\rbrace  \in \mathbb {Z}^d \times \mathbb {Z}^d \mid ||\mathbf {x}-\mathbf {y}||=1 \rbrace ,where || \cdot || denotes the Euclidean norm.A mechanism of a random walk with local memory
is a collection of Markov chains \lbrace M_x\rbrace _{x \in V}
indexed by the vertices of G,
such that the state space of M_x is N(x), the set of neighbors of x.
We denote by p_x(\cdot ,\cdot ) the probability transition function of M_x.A rotor configuration of G is a map \rho :V \rightarrow V  such that \rho (x) is a neighbor of x for all x \in V.
This should be thought of as assigning to each vertex x of G a rotor which points to a neighbor of x via an oriented edge of G.
A walker-and-rotor configuration is a pair (x,\rho ), where x is a vertex of G and \rho  is a rotor configuration of G.Remark 2.1 
A
rotor configuration can be interpreted as either:A function \rho : V \rightarrow V such that \rho (x) \in {N}(x) for all x\in V; or

An oriented subgraph of G that has exactly one outgoing edge of each vertex of G.These two objects are identified with each other by the map
\rho \mapsto (V(\rho ), E(\rho )), whereV(\rho ):=V, \qquad E(\rho ):=\lbrace (x,\rho (x)) \mid x \in V\rbrace .We would like to warn the reader that both interpretations are used interchangeably starting from Section .Definition 2.2 (Random walk with local memory) 
A random walk with local memory, or RWLM for short, is a sequence
(X_n,\rho _n)_{n \ge 0} of walker-and-rotor configurations satisfying the following transition rules:\begin{split}
\rho _{n+1}(x):=&{\mathopen {}\mathclose {\left\lbrace \begin{array}{ll} Y_{n} & \text{if } x=X_n;\\
\rho _{n}(x) & \text{if } x\ne X_n. \end{array}\right.}}; \text{ and }\\
X_{n+1}:=&Y_{n},
\end{split}where Y_{n} is a random neighbor of X_n sampled from p_{X_n}(\rho _n(X_n),\cdot )
independent of the past.Described in words, X_n records the location of the walker and \rho _n records the rotor configuration at time n of the RWLM.
At time n,
the walker updates
the rotor of X_n
using the Markov chain M_{X_n} (which depends only on X_n and \rho _n(X_n)),
and then moves to the vertex to which the new rotor is pointing.
The local memory in the name refers to the fact that the walker records the last exit from each vertex that it visits via the rotor configuration.
An example of a random walk with local memory on \mathbb {Z}^2 is illustrated in Figure REF .
{{figure:cb3621df-65f9-4ddd-b372-4aa1dc2f2ea2}}Note that the dynamics of the RWLM depend on the choice of
the mechanism.
The following are three examples of RWLMs that have appeared in the literature:Aldous-Broder walk {{cite:083c26e57a098ddc4fa122fd6c1d32c9001ee6a1}}, {{cite:425e6a9ea864db70d42418cb4d3890b2bd1e34f9}}, in which
the walker performs a simple random walk on G and the rotor configuration never influences the decision of the walker.
That is to say,
for every x \in V and y \in {N}(x) the measure p_x(y, \cdot ) is the uniform distribution on the neighbors of x.

Rotor walk {{cite:7f4b653c581e259126a32f226c6a9bdef8206e20}}, {{cite:ab835365d958abdfa25f8b8332ff2e094461f4b8}}, {{cite:a2a03e9342a6a478e53f8563511a882fb41a7615}},
in which the Markov chain M_x is given by
a deterministic permutation \tau _x of the neighbors of x.
That is, the chain M_x in state y will transition to \tau _x(y) with probability 1.
We refer to {{cite:3557cbe6fb2accbedd7d02c704f339dd2d229799}}, {{cite:6e15cc63ea41e8a3758547552060c99fa8a4476f}} for more details.

p-rotor walk on \mathbb {Z} {{cite:0fb82fa6e30a9b020cae4b37fdad4dbc4d30a747}} for p\in [0,1], in which the probability transition function p_x (x \in \mathbb {Z}) is
given by
p_x(x\pm 1, x\mp 1)=1-p; \qquad p_x(x\pm 1, x\pm 1)=p.We now present three other examples of RWLMs.Example 2.3 (p-rotor walk on \mathbb {Z}^d) 
Fix d\ge 2 and p\in [0,1].
Denote by \mathbf {e}_1,\ldots , \mathbf {e}_d the canonical basis of \mathbb {R}^d.
The Markov chain M_{\mathbf {x}} (\mathbf {x}\in \mathbb {Z}^d) has state space \lbrace  \mathbf {x}\pm \mathbf {e}_i \mid 1\le i \le d \rbrace  and has the following transition rule:\mathbf {x}\pm \mathbf {e}_i \quad \text{ transitions to } \quad {\mathopen {}\mathclose {\left\lbrace \begin{array}{ll} \mathbf {x}\pm \mathbf {e}_j & \text{with probability $\frac{p}{d-1}$ if $i<j$}; \\
\mathbf {x}\mp \mathbf {e}_j & \text{with probability $\frac{1-p}{d-1}$ if $i<j$};\\
\mathbf {x}\pm \mathbf {e}_j & \text{with probability $\frac{1-p}{d-1}$ if $i>j$};\\
\mathbf {x}\mp \mathbf {e}_j & \text{with probability $\frac{p}{d-1}$ if $i>j$}.
\end{array}\right.}}See Figure REF  for an illustration of this mechanism on \mathbb {Z}^2.
{{figure:f4ebdf9f-49b4-4108-91a8-eaac73bbeda5}}Described in words, if the rotor at the particle's current location is parallel to \mathbf {e}_i,
the walker first picks j uniformly from \lbrace 1,\ldots , d\rbrace  \setminus \lbrace i\rbrace .
Then, the walker rotates the current rotor counterclockwise
in the \lbrace \min (i,j),\max (i,j)\rbrace -plane with probability p, and rotates clockwise
with probability 1-p.Example 2.4 (p,\!q-rotor walk on \mathbb {Z}^d) 
Fix d\ge 2, q\in [0,1], and p\in [0,1].
For each \mathbf {x}\in \mathbb {Z}^d,
the mechanism at \mathbf {x}
transitions according to the mechanism of Aldous-Broder walk with probability q,
and transitions according to the mechanism of p-rotor walk with probability 1-q.
See Figure REF  for an illustration of this mechanism on \mathbb {Z}^2.
{{figure:28edc690-5fc7-4d4b-bd24-a44d3f360131}}Note that we recover `H,V'-walk on \mathbb {Z}^2 in Section 
if p=\frac{1}{2}.
Also note that, unlike for p-rotor walk,
every neighbor of the current location of the walker (all 2d of them) is visited next with positive probability provided that q>0.
Such a walk is called elliptic in the literature of random walks in random environments {{cite:e90d36da0f63598c8f0ad58ca684ed5fcb4958e1}},
which we will explore more in Section .Example 2.5 (Triangular walk) 
The triangular lattice is the graph embedded in \mathbb {R}^2 given by:V&:=\mathopen {}\mathclose {\left\lbrace  a \begin{pmatrix}
1\\0
\end{pmatrix} + b\begin{pmatrix}
1/2 \\ \sqrt{3}/2
\end{pmatrix} \bigg | \, a,b \in \mathbb {Z}\right\rbrace };\\
{E}&:=\lbrace \lbrace \mathbf {x},\mathbf {y}\rbrace  \in V \times V \mid \Vert \mathbf {x}-\mathbf {y}\Vert =1\rbrace .

each with probability \frac{1}{3}.

Random walks with hidden local memory.text:
In this section we present a more general version of random walk with local memory
inspired by hidden Markov chains (see {{cite:35e2ee79971c1ef3fb81c601bfb88f892ad4d748}} for references on hidden Markov chains).
We remark that the content of this section is independent of the later sections.For each x \in V, a hidden mechanism at x is a Markov chain M_x with finite state space S_x and probability transition function p_x(\cdot ,\cdot ).
A jump rule is a map f_x:S_x \rightarrow \mathcal {P}({N}(x)) from S_x to the set of probability distributions on the set of neighbors of x.
A hidden state configuration is a map \kappa : V \rightarrow \sqcup _{x \in V} S_x such that \kappa (x) \in S_x for all x \in V.Definition 4.1 (Random walk with hidden local memory) 
A random walk with hidden local memory, or RWHLM for short, is a sequence
(X_n, \rho _n, \kappa _n)_{n \ge 0} satisfying the following transition rules:\kappa _{n+1}(x):={\mathopen {}\mathclose {\left\lbrace \begin{array}{ll} K_n & \text{if } x=X_n;\\
\kappa _{n}(x) & \text{if } x\ne X_n. \end{array}\right.}};

 \rho _{n+1}(x):={\mathopen {}\mathclose {\left\lbrace \begin{array}{ll} Y_n & \text{if } x=X_n;\\
\rho _{n}(x) & \text{if } x\ne X_n, \end{array}\right.}}

X_{n+1}:=Y_n,where K_n is a random element of S_{X_n} sampled from p_{X_n}(\kappa _{n}(X_n), \cdot )
independent of the past, and Y_n is a random neighbor of x sampled from f_{X_n}(K_n) independent of the past.Described in words,
at each time step (i) the walker first updates the hidden state
of its current location using the given hidden mechanism.
Then, (ii) the walker updates the rotor of its current location by sampling the new rotor from the probability distribution corresponding to the new hidden state.
Finally, (iii) the walker travels to the vertex specified by the new rotor.Example 4.2 (Hidden triangular walk)  Let G be the triangular lattice.
For each \mathbf {x}\in V, the hidden mechanism at \mathbf {x}\in V
has the following state space and transition probability:S_{\mathbf {x}}:=\lbrace  s_1,s_2,s_3 \rbrace ;\qquad p_\mathbf {x}:=\begin{bmatrix}
0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2}\\
0 & 0 & 1\\
1 &0 &0
\end{bmatrix}.That is, s_1 transitions to either s_2 or s_3 with equal probability, s_2 transitions to s_3 with probability 1, and s_3 transitions to s_1 with probability 1.We now describe the jump rule f_\mathbf {x}.
Let N_1 \sqcup N_2 be the partition of the neighbors {N}(\mathbf {x}) of \mathbf {x} given by:N_1:= \mathbf {x}+\mathopen {}\mathclose {\left\lbrace \begin{pmatrix}
1\\ 0
\end{pmatrix}, \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}
-{1} \\ {\sqrt{3}}
\end{pmatrix} , \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}
-1 \\ {-\sqrt{3}}
\end{pmatrix}\right\rbrace }; \qquad N_2:=\mathbf {x}+ \mathopen {}\mathclose {\left\lbrace \begin{pmatrix}
-1\\0
\end{pmatrix},\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}
1 \\ {\sqrt{3}}
\end{pmatrix}, \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}
1\\ -\sqrt{3}
\end{pmatrix}\right\rbrace }.The distribution f_\mathbf {x}(s_1) is then given by the uniform distribution on N_1,
while f_\mathbf {x}(s_2) and f_\mathbf {x}(s_3) are the uniform distribution on N_2.
{{figure:e2f325a7-efab-45c4-89b1-18b30771da14}}Without knowing the hidden states, an outside observer will not be able to predict the future dynamics of this RWHLM even while knowing the past and present location of the walker and rotor configuration, as illustrated in Figure REF .Note that a non-hidden RWLM is a special case of RWHLM,
with S_x (x \in V) being the set of neighbors of x and with
f_x(y) (y \in {N}(x)) being the probability distribution concentrated on y.
On the other hand,
any RWHLM on a simple graph G can be emulated by a non-hidden RWLM on a larger graph (with multiple edges) in the following manner.Let G^\times  be the undirected graph
with
vertex set V(G)
and with an edge incident to x and y in G^\times  for each \lbrace x,y\rbrace \in E(G) and each hidden state s \in S_x of the RWHLM.
Such an edge is labeled e({x,y,s}).For any x \in V(G^\times ), the mechanism of this RWLM on x is the Markov chain with state space the set of edges incident to x in G^\times  (instead of the set of neighbors of x), and with probability transition functionp_x^\times (e({x,y,s}),e({x,y^{\prime },s^{\prime }})) := p_{x}(s,s^{\prime })\, (f_x(s^{\prime }))(y^{\prime }),where p_x and f_x are the probability transition function and the jump rule for the RWHLM, respectively.This RWLM on G^\times  emulates the RWHLM on G in the following sense.
Let (X_n,\rho _n,\kappa _n)_{n \ge 0} be an RWHLM on G.
Start an RWLM (X_n^\times , \rho _n^\times )_{n \ge 0} on G^\times  with the following initial configuration:X_0^\times &:= X_0; \qquad \rho ^\times _0(x):= e({x, \rho _0(x), \kappa _0(x))} \quad (x \in V).Then (X_n, \rho _n)_{n \ge 0} is equal in distribution to
(X_n^\times , h(\rho _n^\times ))_{n \ge 0},
where h(\rho _n^\times ) is the rotor configuration of G
given by h(\rho _n^\times )(x):=y if \rho _n^\times (x)=e({x,y,s}) for some s \in S_x.As a consequence of this reduction, we can convert any hidden triangular walk from Example REF  to a non-hidden random walk with local memory, and then apply a version of Proposition REF  for non-simple graphs to conclude that the scaling limit of this hidden triangular walk is a standard Brownian motion in \mathbb {R}^2.Since any RWHLM can be emulated by an RWLM on another (nonsimple) graph,

A random walk with hidden local memory, or RWHLM for short, is a sequence
(X_n, \rho _n, \kappa _n)_{n \ge 0} satisfying the following transition rules:\kappa _{n+1}(x):={\mathopen {}\mathclose {\left\lbrace \begin{array}{ll} K_n & \text{if } x=X_n;\\
\kappa _{n}(x) & \text{if } x\ne X_n. \end{array}\right.}};

 \rho _{n+1}(x):={\mathopen {}\mathclose {\left\lbrace \begin{array}{ll} Y_n & \text{if } x=X_n;\\
\rho _{n}(x) & \text{if } x\ne X_n, \end{array}\right.}}

X_{n+1}:=Y_n,where K_n is a random element of S_{X_n} sampled from p_{X_n}(\kappa _{n}(X_n), \cdot )
independent of the past, and Y_n is a random neighbor of x sampled from f_{X_n}(K_n) independent of the past.Described in words,
at each time step (i) the walker first updates the hidden state
of its current location using the given hidden mechanism.
Then, (ii) the walker updates the rotor of its current location by sampling the new rotor from the probability distribution corresponding to the new hidden state.
Finally, (iii) the walker travels to the vertex specified by the new rotor.Example 4.2 (Hidden triangular walk)  Let G be the triangular lattice.
For each \mathbf {x}\in V, the hidden mechanism at \mathbf {x}\in V
has the following state space and transition probability:S_{\mathbf {x}}:=\lbrace  s_1,s_2,s_3 \rbrace ;\qquad p_\mathbf {x}:=\begin{bmatrix}
0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2}\\
0 & 0 & 1\\
1 &0 &0
\end{bmatrix}.That is, s_1 transitions to either s_2 or s_3 with equal probability, s_2 transitions to s_3 with probability 1, and s_3 transitions to s_1 with probability 1.We now describe the jump rule f_\mathbf {x}.
Let N_1 \sqcup N_2 be the partition of the neighbors {N}(\mathbf {x}) of \mathbf {x} given by:N_1:= \mathbf {x}+\mathopen {}\mathclose {\left\lbrace \begin{pmatrix}
1\\ 0
\end{pmatrix}, \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}
-{1} \\ {\sqrt{3}}
\end{pmatrix} , \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}
-1 \\ {-\sqrt{3}}
\end{pmatrix}\right\rbrace }; \qquad N_2:=\mathbf {x}+ \mathopen {}\mathclose {\left\lbrace \begin{pmatrix}
-1\\0
\end{pmatrix},\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}
1 \\ {\sqrt{3}}
\end{pmatrix}, \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}
1\\ -\sqrt{3}
\end{pmatrix}\right\rbrace }.The distribution f_\mathbf {x}(s_1) is then given by the uniform distribution on N_1,
while f_\mathbf {x}(s_2) and f_\mathbf {x}(s_3) are the uniform distribution on N_2.
{{figure:e2f325a7-efab-45c4-89b1-18b30771da14}}Without knowing the hidden states, an outside observer will not be able to predict the future dynamics of this RWHLM even while knowing the past and present location of the walker and rotor configuration, as illustrated in Figure REF .Note that a non-hidden RWLM is a special case of RWHLM,
with S_x (x \in V) being the set of neighbors of x and with
f_x(y) (y \in {N}(x)) being the probability distribution concentrated on y.
On the other hand,
any RWHLM on a simple graph G can be emulated by a non-hidden RWLM on a larger graph (with multiple edges) in the following manner.Let G^\times  be the undirected graph
with
vertex set V(G)
and with an edge incident to x and y in G^\times  for each \lbrace x,y\rbrace \in E(G) and each hidden state s \in S_x of the RWHLM.
Such an edge is labeled e({x,y,s}).For any x \in V(G^\times ), the mechanism of this RWLM on x is the Markov chain with state space the set of edges incident to x in G^\times  (instead of the set of neighbors of x), and with probability transition functionp_x^\times (e({x,y,s}),e({x,y^{\prime },s^{\prime }})) := p_{x}(s,s^{\prime })\, (f_x(s^{\prime }))(y^{\prime }),where p_x and f_x are the probability transition function and the jump rule for the RWHLM, respectively.This RWLM on G^\times  emulates the RWHLM on G in the following sense.
Let (X_n,\rho _n,\kappa _n)_{n \ge 0} be an RWHLM on G.
Start an RWLM (X_n^\times , \rho _n^\times )_{n \ge 0} on G^\times  with the following initial configuration:X_0^\times &:= X_0; \qquad \rho ^\times _0(x):= e({x, \rho _0(x), \kappa _0(x))} \quad (x \in V).Then (X_n, \rho _n)_{n \ge 0} is equal in distribution to
(X_n^\times , h(\rho _n^\times ))_{n \ge 0},
where h(\rho _n^\times ) is the rotor configuration of G
given by h(\rho _n^\times )(x):=y if \rho _n^\times (x)=e({x,y,s}) for some s \in S_x.As a consequence of this reduction, we can convert any hidden triangular walk from Example REF  to a non-hidden random walk with local memory, and then apply a version of Proposition REF  for non-simple graphs to conclude that the scaling limit of this hidden triangular walk is a standard Brownian motion in \mathbb {R}^2.Since any RWHLM can be emulated by an RWLM on another (nonsimple) graph,
the rest of the paper will be focused on studying the latter (albeit on simple graphs).

\lbrace H \in 2^{E(G)} \mid B \subseteq H\rbrace , where B is a finite subset of E(G). An electrical network is a pair (G,c), where G is a locally finite, simple, connected graph, and
c:E \rightarrow \mathbb {R}_{>0} is a function that sends each unoriented edge of G to a positive real number. We denote by c\lbrace x,y\rbrace  the conductance of the unoriented edge \lbrace x,y\rbrace .The electrical network (G,c) is associated to the Markov chain with state space V(G) in which the probability to transition from x to y is equal to
\frac{c\lbrace x,y\rbrace }{\sum _{z \in {N}(x)} c\lbrace x,z\rbrace } for any x \in V(G) and y \in {N}(x).
This Markov chain is called the network random walk on (G,c).
The network (G,c) is recurrent if the network random walk eventually returns to its starting point with probability 1, and is transient otherwise.We start by defining the wired spanning forest for the network (G,c) when G is a finite graph, in which case the distribution is concentrated on the spanning trees of G.Definition 5.2 
Let (G,c) be an electrical network such that G is a finite graph. The weight of a subgraph H of G is\Xi (H):=\prod _{\lbrace x,y\rbrace  \in E(H)} c\lbrace x,y\rbrace .Definition 5.3 (Unoriented wired spanning forest for finite graphs) 
Let (G,c) be an electrical network such that G is a finite graph.
The unoriented wired spanning forest \operatorname{\mathsf {{WSF}}}:=\operatorname{\mathsf {{WSF}}}(G,c) is the probability distribution on spanning trees of G in which each tree T is picked with probability proportional to \Xi (T).We now define the wired spanning forest for infinite graphs using the concept of wired exhaustion.Definition 5.4 (Wired exhaustion) 
Let (G,c) be an electrical network.
Let (W_n)_{n \ge 0} be a sequence of finite, connected subsets of V(G) such that\bigcup _{n \ge 0}W_n=V(G); and

W_n \subseteq W_{n+1} for all n \ge 0.The wired exhaustion of G is the sequence of electrical networks (G_n, c_n)_{n \ge 0} defined as follows.
The graph G_n is the undirected graph obtained from G by identifying all the vertices of V(G)\setminus W_n to a single vertex z_n and removing loops and extra multiple edges that are formed.
The conductance c_n: E(G_n) \rightarrow \mathbb {R}_{>0} is defined byc_n\lbrace x,y\rbrace := {\mathopen {}\mathclose {\left\lbrace \begin{array}{ll}
c\lbrace x,y\rbrace & \text{ if } x,y \in W_n;\\

\end{array}\right.}}We denote by \mu _n the probability distribution \operatorname{\mathsf {{WSF}}}(G_n,c_n) on the subgraphs of G_n.Definition 5.5 (Unoriented wired spanning forest for infinite graphs) 
Let (G,c) be an electrical network. The wired spanning forest {\operatorname{\mathsf {{WSF}}}}:={\operatorname{\mathsf {{WSF}}}}(G,c) is a probability distribution on subgraphs of G such that, for any wired exhaustion and any finite B \subseteq E(G),\operatorname{\mathsf {{WSF}}}[B\subseteq F] = \lim _{n \rightarrow \infty } \mu _n[B \subseteq T_n],where F is a random subgraph of G distributed according to \operatorname{\mathsf {{WSF}}} and T_n is a random spanning tree of G_n distributed according to \mu _n.The quantity \mu _n[B \subseteq T_n] increases as n \rightarrow \infty  {{cite:fa85d0121ee6d02ada9933b43966673f9811277b}}, and hence
the limit in equation (REF ) exists and does not depend on the choice of the wired exhaustion.

We conclude with a few natural questions.By Theorem , if the RWLM starts at the origin
and satisfies ,  and , then the trajectory of the walker

for almost every initial rotor configuration picked from the distribution {{\operatorname{\mathsf {{WSF}}}}^+_{\operatorname{\mathbf {0}}}(G,c).
Can this be extended to include all initial rotor configurations?

In particular, a positive answer to this question will give us a scaling limit result for p-rotor walk on Zd (d2) when p=12.


An RWLM is recurrent if every vertex is visited infinitely often by the walker a.s. and is transient otherwise.
A consequence of Theorem  is that all d-dimensional RWLMs satisfying conditions in
Theorem 
are transient if d\ge 3.
Is it true that these RWLMs are recurrent if d=2?

Consider p-rotor walk on \mathbb {Z}^d with p\in (0,1) and d\ge 2.
What is the scaling factor for the trajectory (X_n)_{n\ge 0} of the walker of this RWLM?
What does its scaling limit look like?
Is this RWLM recurrent?
Note that the case d=1 is resolved in
{{cite:0fb82fa6e30a9b020cae4b37fdad4dbc4d30a747}}, where it is shown that this RWLM is recurrent and that
\mathopen {}\mathclose {\left\lbrace  \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} X_{\lfloor nt\rfloor },t \ge 0\right\rbrace }
converges weakly to a 1-dimensional perturbed Brownian motion.
We are not aware of any definition of d-dimensional perturbed Brownian motions for d\ge 2 in the literature.
